#9828. Operação de influência russa tem como alvo generalizado a América Latina

A operação, que contou com o uso de inteligência artificial, utilizou e-mails falsos, documentos governamentais falsificados e a criação de uma organização local para atacar escolas no Peru e no Equador, entre outras ações.

This translation was generated with our internal AI tool.

Uma operação de influência sediada na Rússia enviou e-mails se passando por autoridades educacionais do Peru e do Equador, levando algumas escolas a realizar eventos que os operadores então utilizaram para alimentar controvérsias, de acordo com um relatório divulgado pela OpenAI.

A operação de “fachada falsa”, apelidada de “Dark Clark,” utilizou uma combinação de planejamento baseado em IA e relatórios, além de técnicas mais tradicionais, para convencer administradores escolares a celebrar um “Dia Nacional da Diversidade Cultural e Linguística” em 21 de maio e a destacar três figuras políticas ucranianas, que foram então usadas para tentar semear divisão, afirmou a OpenAI em uma análise do uso operacional de seus modelos de IA. Em outras campanhas, como as direcionadas à Argentina e à Bolívia, as operações russas pareciam ter como objetivo influenciar a política local.

Related:Artex: The AI Pen-Test Tool Hackers Turned Into a Weapon

Os supostos operadores russos utilizaram IA para tornar seu fluxo de trabalho mais eficiente, redigindo relatórios internos sobre suas atividades e, em alguns casos, criando conteúdo para suas campanhas, informou a empresa.

“A IA pode conferir a essas operações de fachada maior escala, eficiência, fluência linguística e capacidade editorial”, afirmou a OpenAI em sua análise. “Os operadores podem usar essas vantagens para explorar vítimas desavisadas, como funcionários ou editores, e divulgar seu conteúdo para públicos que não têm ideia de quem está por trás disso, nem quais são suas motivações.”

A América Latina tornou-se um palco cibernético de espionagem e operações de influência na disputa entre as principais potências globais, tornando-se a região mais atacada ciberneticamente no mundo. Atores conhecidos ligados à China tiveram como alvo tanto a Venezuela quanto o Panamá no início deste ano para obter informações sobre a política na região e proteger os interesses petrolíferos do país. A Rússia expandiu suas operações de inteligência cibernética e desinformação, principalmente para frustrar os esforços dos EUA na região, de acordo com um relatório da RAND de 2026.

“A Rússia também mantém capacidades cibernéticas para realizar invasões direcionadas e desinformação com o objetivo de semear divisão política, perturbar a percepção da situação e enfraquecer as mensagens dos EUA em situações de crise”, afirmou o relatório da RAND.

A operação russa parece estar ligada a uma entidade conhecida como “Politology” ou “La Compania”, que tem vínculos com o falecido oligarca russo Yevgeniy Prigozhin, com o objetivo de influenciar a política global, de acordo com a análise da OpenAI. Os relatórios fornecidos ao modelo de IA continham informações detalhadas sobre as operações do grupo, incluindo detalhes sobre trabalhos anteriores que os ligavam aos grupos de Prigozhin.

Related:CISA Announces Enhanced Reporting Form for Cyber Incidents

O ataque de desinformação contra escolas em Lima, no Peru, foi uma das campanhas descritas pelos atacantes. Ao elaborar uma diretiva com aparência oficial para os administradores escolares, citando um fictício “Dia da Diversidade Cultural e Linguística”, eles solicitaram que os alunos participassem de atividades de 10 a 15 minutos para aprender sobre três figuras políticas ucranianas. Posteriormente, os operadores instruíram os administradores a enviar fotos do evento.

A OpenAI investigou os eventos e encontrou detalhes que corroboravam as alegações dos operadores, disse Ben Nimmo, pesquisador-chefe da equipe de inteligência e investigações da OpenAI, à Dark Reading. O Ministério da Educação do Peru emitiu uma carta oficial (em espanhol) dois meses depois, mencionando a diretiva e informando que a embaixada da Ucrânia havia identificado a fraude em sua própria carta, datada de 25 de maio.

Related:Philippine Migrant Worker Data Likely Leaked in 69GB Government Breach

“Nunca se deve acreditar em um agente de ameaças pelo que ele diz, certo?”, diz Nimmo. “ Para cada alegação, buscamos evidências na internet que a corroborassem. Para algumas das alegações que eles fizeram, simplesmente não conseguimos encontrar evidências. Talvez tenham sido removidas, talvez estivessem em lugares que não seriam encontrados por meio de uma busca em fontes abertas, talvez nunca tenham acontecido.”

Uma diretiva fraudulenta enviada às escolas de Lima, no Peru, por supostos agentes de desinformação russos. Fonte: Ministério da Educação do Peru (traduzido pelo Claude Opus 5.5)

Como a operação resultou em um político na Polônia citando os eventos, a OpenAI classificou o sucesso com nota 5 na Escala de Impacto de Operações de Influência de seis pontos.

Os operadores russos usaram técnicas semelhantes para induzir escolas no Equador a realizar uma cerimônia de juramento de lealdade ao presidente Daniel Noboa e a Erik Prince, ex-chefe da empresa militar privada Blackwater, afirmou a OpenAI em sua análise. Algumas escolas seguiram a orientação, o que levou a cobertura jornalística e uma denúncia oficial por parte do Ministro da Educação.

Os operadores alegaram ter conduzido com sucesso outras operações de influência das quais a OpenAI não conseguiu encontrar evidências, incluindo a divulgação de uma história de que uma influenciadora brasileira nas redes sociais teria sido traficada para a Ucrânia e a disseminação de um trecho de áudio que alegava que bancos bolivianos pretendiam limitar saques em dinheiro. Os operadores também, ocasionalmente, pediam ao ChatGPT para encontrar incidentes regionais pelos quais pudessem assumir o crédito, diz Nimmo.

Os operadores russos criaram uma chamada “plataforma de pesquisa”, denominada Social Research Center, que contratava funcionários regionais para criar conteúdo local, sem que eles soubessem que a organização fazia parte de uma iniciativa de desinformação.

Embora as operações tivessem como alvo a América Latina, a intenção era prejudicar as relações entre a Ucrânia e o resto do mundo, afirma Nimmo, da OpenAI.

“A maneira como eu encaro essa operação como um todo é que ela gira em torno da Ucrânia”, diz ele. “Trata-se de fazer a Ucrânia parecer mal.”

De modo geral, o uso da IA não abriu novos caminhos para ataques nem criou novas oportunidades de desinformação, mas a tecnologia fez com que as traduções para o idioma nativo soassem mais naturais, permitiu que os operadores assumissem papéis específicos com mais facilidade e simplificou o fluxo de trabalho da operação, afirma Nimmo.

“Se você pensar na Agência de Pesquisa na Internet e no inglês desleixado deles, acho que a IA realmente oferece uma vantagem incremental”, diz ele. “Mas não tenho a impressão de que o uso do nosso modelo tenha sido o fator decisivo. De certa forma, o manual de táticas era muito, muito tradicional.”

#9826. Lock your GitHub Actions

GitHub Actions now supports workflow lockfiles.

Because GitHub Actions are fetched from Git, the previous advice was to pin to a full SHA instead of a tag. This is because tags are mutable and susceptible to supply-chain attacks where an attacker points a previously safe tag at malicious code.

Install the gh-actions-lock extension to the gh CLI:

The workflow now uses vX.Y.Z tags and looks like this:

And it generates a lockfile at .github/workflows/actions.lock:

Commit modified workflows and the new lockfile.

Good news, both already support lockfiles! Your periodic updates will also update the lockfile. Remember to use cooldowns.

GitHub also recommends verifying lockfiles in CI to ensure it’s up-to-date and not corrupt.

They suggest copying this verify-lockfile.yml into your repo. I decided to put it into my existing lint workflow, but in its own job so it runs independently and in parallel:

Note I’m using the lightweight ubuntu-slim runner here. Also, it’s pinning to v0.4.1; we’ll have to update that at some point or figure out a way to automate it. That’s for another time.

Don’t forget that we just modified the actions in a workflow, so need to relock with gh actions-lock. Nothing actually changes if adding to lint.yml because it’s already locking actions/checkout. But if you created a new file like verify-lockfile.yml, you’ll need to relock for that. The CI will let you know.

zizmor is a security linter for GitHub Actions and strongly recommended. If you don’t use it, please do.

Versions before v1.32.0 tell you to hash-pin actions, and v1.32.0 is the first to support lockfiles.

I use zizmor in prek, so add/update zizmor in .pre-commit-config.yaml:

#9825. Give Your Coding Agents a Memory You Own

I work across several machines, and I switch coding agents depending on the task. Every one of them meets my projects as a stranger. The reasoning from “last Tuesday” disappears when the session ends. Each new agent, on each new host, starts from zero.

Earlier this year, Software Forgets: Agent Traces Are the Memory made the case that coding agents already produce the record we keep losing. As they search a codebase, try approaches, hit errors, read documentation, and change direction, they leave behind a dense account of not just what changed, but why.

While the diagnosis is correct, traces are only potential memory. The session logs of an agent are still just an archive. You cannot grep your way to “why did we move off the streaming parser?” across ten thousand turns. For an agent to use those traces while it works, they need indexing, retrieval, ranking, and exact provenance.

That is what funes provides. It is a durable memory layer for your agents (Claude Code, Codex, pi, and Hermes). It is built from the sessions already on your machine. It works locally and becomes part of your agent's normal workflow with one command. When you want it to, it can also travel to a Hugging Face dataset you own, private by default.

funes is a single binary. Its default inference backend has no ML runtime dependency, and embedding and reranking happen on your machine. Install it:

That one add command builds the first index, gives the agent recall and get tools, and installs the automation that indexes each completed turn. Indexing is incremental, with new runs adding new turns rather than embedding the whole history again. The older and deeper content can backfill in bounded steps.

From there, you just work. When a task touches a past decision, rationale, or finding, the agent can reach for recall itself. You do not need to remember the old session or paste its context into the new one.

With funes added, recall happens inside the conversation. The agent reaches for its memory on its own and names the session behind its answer.

recall returns the original text, not a summary, and shows exactly where it came from (the agent, timestamp, session, and turn). Each result includes a get command that opens the full turn and its surrounding context.

Underneath, one deterministic pipeline parses every supported trace into the same turn-and-block shape, chunks it, embeds it with a pinned local model, and writes it to a local Lance dataset. A query combines vector and BM25 search, fuses their rankings, reranks the candidates with a cross-encoder, reweights them by recency, and attaches neighboring chunks.

That design gives funes three important properties:

The agent as a stranger problem is already solved on one machine. But memory gets more useful when the next agent is running somewhere else.

To make a memory follow your work, bind one when you add funes to an agent:

The bind publishes your current memory there. funes then keeps it current, indexing each turn locally and publishing at session boundaries. The agent recalls from it throughout. Run the same command on another machine and the memory follows you there.

Underneath, the local memory is a Lance dataset, and the shared memory is a Hugging Face dataset (private by default) you own.

Before anything reaches the Hub, credentials have already been redacted during indexing. Publishing then scans every chunk again and withholds anything that still looks like a secret. The scanner behind this is documented in SECURITY.md, including what it does and doesn't cover.

When an agent reads a remote memory, funes caches the dataset files locally, so warm queries return to local speed. The Hub supplies the ownership, access control, versioning, and distribution it already supplies for other datasets. Your memory does not become an account in a separate memory service, and you do not rent it back through an API.

recall is shaped for agents. When you want to put a question to a memory yourself, use ask. It reads your local memory by default:

Or point it at a shared memory. We published a memory of funes development, so you can ask why funes works the way it does without creating a memory of your own:

funes ask is the read-only, one-question sibling of funes add. It recalls the passages, hands them to a coding agent, and returns a grounded answer that names its sources. It does not install an integration or change the agent's persistent setup.

A retrieval miss is not papered over. If the passages do not support an answer, the agent says so. You can rephrase the question or add funes to the agent so it can search the memory iteratively during normal work.

A shared memory is not tied to the agent or model that created it. Start a task in Claude Code, continue it in Codex next week, and the second agent can recall the first agent's reasoning. Use pi with a local model or one served through the Hugging Face router, then return to Claude.

Claude makes a decision; a hook indexes it; Codex recalls it in another session. The older hits in the demo are earlier recordings of the same experiment: an append-only memory remembered the rehearsals too.

Published memories carry a dataset card and the funes tag, making them recognizable and discoverable on the Hub. The Hub already hosts open weights and datasets. funes adds open working memory. It holds the decisions, failed approaches, and rationale behind a project, queryable by another agent and traceable to the sessions that produced them.

A long investigation bloats a session until each turn costs more to carry the context than to do the work. The usual answers are to let the agent compact and carry on, or to write a handoff and start fresh. Recall is a third, so we measured them against each other on the handoff-vs-recall benchmark: two tasks whose answer cannot be reconstructed without the session prior knowledge.

Compaction is what most agents do by default, and it was the only one of the three whose result divided: it arrived on one task and never arrived on the other. Where it failed, its summary had flattened the findings that mattered. Recall returns the passages themselves, so a finding does not have to survive summarization.

Recall was the cheapest of the three on both tasks, 8x cheaper than a written handoff on one and 4x on the other.

The lighter segment of each bar is the one-time charge for preparing the channel, the handoff or the compaction, paid before the first question is asked and counted once. A cross marks a channel that never arrives, and so has no cost per success.

“To think is to forget differences, generalize, make abstractions.” — Jorge Luis Borges, Funes the Memorious

Your agents already wrote the record. funes lives at github.com/huggingface/funes, one command away from turning that record into a memory the next agent can read, on whichever machine you happen to be on.

funes invents little of this. It leans on open-source embedding models good enough to run locally, on Lance's append-only datasets with cheap incremental writes, and on the Hub's caching and content-dedup for datasets. The work is in fitting them into a memory an agent can actually use.

funes is open source too. Open an issue for anything from an install snag to a recall that missed, or an agent you'd like supported.

Ran funes 1.3.0 on a machine with 19,195 coding-agent sessions already on disk (LongMemEval laid down in the real ~/.claude and ~/.codex layouts), 100 questions whose answer sits in exactly one session, scored by whether that session comes back. Disclosure: I maintain deja-vu, one of the tools in the same table.

Full index: 2h03m on an M4 pro laptop (308k chunks), 6.3s per query. With defaults: hit@1 9/100, hit@5 39, found@50 71. With --half-life 0: 19/46/71 — the 30-day recency half-life halves rank-1 on history older than a month, which is most of what's on a real disk; worth a mention in the docs. Once recency is off, the vector+rerank stack is clearly the best ranker in the table at rank five. The documented one-minute first pass leaves 218 of the 19k sessions indexed (0/100 answered), so the "about a minute" framing is really "about a minute until the embedding job starts".

For comparison on the same corpus, deja-vu (plain BM25 over 24 agents' files) indexes in 29s and answers in 24ms at hit@1 18/100, hit@5 35. Corpus, drivers and every row: vshulcz.github.io/deja-vu/guide/day-zero.html - happy to be corrected if a setting I missed changes the numbers.

longmemeval does not really need semantic search: BM25 already gives the same ratio you mentioned IIRC, so for this use case this is pretty much expected that it is not worth paying the cost of evaluating the embeddings (this extra cost you see at indexing and recall time). funes shines when the information is actually difficult to find.

#9824. UK Warns Its Critical Infrastructure Faces Grave Risk

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Britain's new Labour-led government is making a concerted push to get ahead of the AI risks to its national networks and the industrial complex.

At various levels of the United Kingdom government, officials are warning about the threat of cyberattacks against its critical infrastructure.

His Majesty's Government broadcast its cybersecurity agenda on Nov. 3, releasing a variety of policy papers, an annual report from its lead cybersecurity agency, and related announcements pertaining to the security of small and medium-sized businesses (SMBs), supply chain vendors, critical national infrastructure (CNI), and more. These items all followed from an updated Autumn Budget 2026, released last week, which provisioned nearly two hundred billion pounds for AI-driven government cybersecurity projects.

Amid all of the practical policy updates, the headline quote of the day came from the state's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), which assessed that it's "highly likely that between now and 2028, AI‑powered malware will have been used in a ransomware attack on UK CNI." It also labeled "highly likely" the prospect that "China, Russia, and other nation states will routinely use AI cyber to achieve their geopolitical goals" in the country.

Related:Japan Pushes Emergency Funding for Cybersecurity as AI-Assisted Breaches Rise

In a new report, Manchester-based NCC Group polled Members of Parliament (MPs) about the state of the UK's CNI cybersecurity posture. About half (51%) of MPs reported that their areas of the country are "not keeping pace" with the threats to its infrastructure. Only 22% expressed confidence in their country's posture. Asked about the nation's ability to fight off a major attack against its CNI, 47% believe that it's unprepared, whereas 41% feel it is.

The survey data is best read as aspirational, not prescriptive. There's little evidence that the UK is less prepared than other nations in addressing threats to its critical infrastructure, or that politicians would be able to tell one way or the other. Leaders are simply aware of the magnitude of what faces them.

"The challenge isn't a lack of government action; it's proof that action translates into resilience," says Katharina Sommer, head of government affairs at NCC Group. "There's still no tested blueprint for coordinating cyber response effectively across government and industry, and that’s not a problem unique to the UK. The test for critical infrastructure operators is whether they can demonstrate, before an attack hits, that they can sustain essential services, recover quickly and maintain public confidence," which remains an open question.

A clearer message came through on Nov. 3, from the experts at the NCSC. Using a scale in which "likely" accords with roughly 55% to 75% odds, "highly likely" with 80% to 90% odds, and "almost certain" approaching 100%, it bet that it is:

Related:UK Wades Into Tech Sovereignty Amid AI Policy Changes

Likely that threat actors will use AI cyber tools to needle vulnerabilities in CNI

Highly likely that nation-states will use AI to increase the speed and sophistication of their cyberattacks, in service of their geopolitical goals in the UK; in particular, the agency identified China as the foremost player in terms of intent and capability to hit CNI and other strategic targets

Almost certain that "many systems will remain vulnerable" to AI-empowered attacks

The NCSC also drew out some future scenarios. Optimistically, it acknowledged that AI-driven cyber threat development might slow, allowing a window of time for the UK to catch up with the problem. Pessimistically, it painted a picture in which AI threats totally outpace the UK's ability to keep up.

"The situation is likely to be worse than is currently known, with many variables and unknowns still to be discovered," according to the report.

The message out of the UK government on Tuesday was, more or less: we're trying to get ahead of this.

In a policy paper, the government acknowledged that 2018's Network and Information Systems (NIS) Regulations — the UK's only multisector cybersecurity law — is "out of date and insufficient to tackle the threats we face." In a speech announcing its Annual Review 2026, NCSC CEO Richard Horne called the law built to replace NIS 2018 — November 2025's Cyber Security and Resilience Bill — "a vital step forward." The updated bill brings data centers, managed service providers (MSPs), and specific "critical suppliers" into the fold, and introduces stricter breach reporting requirements and hefty fines for negligence.

Related:Third Serengeti Sweep Tops 1,400 Arrests as Investigations Mature

In a separate policy paper concerning the same bill, the government stated its intention to introduce a new vendor risk management framework focused specifically on the "national security risks posed by vendors" connected to essential service providers. And in yet a third, related paper, the government described how the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill will be used to account for agentic "loss of control" incidents, in the fashion of this summer's AI industry lab leaks. Projected future measures include:

Security and resilience requirements to prevent loss of control incidents

Empowering ministers to perform postmortems

The bill is currently passing through Parliament.

Besides this one bill, the UK government also announced £2.4 billion in subsidies to help micro-, small, and medium-sized businesses attain "Cyber Essentials" certifications. All of this week's announcements come on the heels of an Autumn Budget last week, which arranged for tens of billions of pounds each to fund, among other things:

A National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre, for vulnerability discovery across the country, including CNI

A National Cyber Shield, for training AI agents to automate cyber defense

A separate National Agentic Security Unit for fighting rogue AI agents

"Increasing the funding and focus on cybersecurity to help keep the UK secure is very welcome," says Jack Chapman, senior vice president of threat intelligence for KnowBe4. At the same time, he adds, "the main challenge I see is scale."

"£154 million for cyber-defenses is a good step," he believes, "but the NCSC estimates cyberattacks cost UK organizations £14.7 billion a year."

Dark Reading asked cybersecurity experts what governments like the UK's need to do to prevent future worst-case scenarios. They consistently emphasized the same point:

"AI did not create new weaknesses; it revealed them. Most incidents still start through the same familiar routes, such as phishing, stolen credentials, and the traditional kill chain paths attackers have relied on for years. The key to stopping these threats is, surprisingly, not exciting: it's the fundamentals," Chapman argues.

The fundamentals for Graham Taylor CBE, director of defense strategy for Northern Europe at OPSWAT, start with protecting the edge. "Too many critical sites rely on firewalls and VPNs for connections that only need to send data one way. Where a facility only exports monitoring data, a hardware-enforced data diode removes the return path entirely, so neither a human attacker nor AI can use that link to send commands into the facility," he says.

Jacob Krell, Suzu Labs senior director for secure AI solutions and cybersecurity, emphasizes network segmentation "built like a boat." AI is going to make the perimeter easier to breach, he says, "and it cuts the time to objective once an attacker is inside. Critical infrastructure is notoriously vulnerable here because operators are hesitant to patch and test systems, and their caution is rational; a bad update takes a plant offline. So the perimeter fails more often and the interior offers nothing to slow lateral movement."

John Strand, owner of Black Hills Information Security, tosses out a less conventional suggestion for fighting off AI threats to CNI. "If AI gives attackers the ability to do a tremendous amount of work very quickly, defenders have an opportunity to present them with large numbers of decoys to investigate," he says. "We need creative ways to make those decoys look realistic and dynamic. The more time attacking AI agents spend interacting with decoys, the less time they spend attacking real systems."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

InfoQ Homepage News JioHotstar Benchmarks Knowledge Bases for AI Coding Agents

Nov 11, 2026 2 min read

JioHotstar evaluated six approaches to helping AI coding agents navigate large codebases, finding that structural code search performed well on clearly defined engineering tasks, while semantic retrieval helped more with ambiguous requirements. The evaluation also found that adding retrieval layers did not consistently improve task completion or reduce token consumption.

Abhishek Bansal, Senior Staff Engineer at JioHotStar, compared filesystem tools, Sourcebot, Graphify, CocoIndex Code, Repowise, and an in-house retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline. The team evaluated the approaches using subsets of SWE-bench and CodeScaleBench, alongside a custom question-answering harness for JioHotstar's codebase. The experiments used Claude Sonnet as the solving model and measured task accuracy, token consumption, agent turns, and tool usability.

JioHotstar’s benchmark setup for evaluating code retrieval approaches for AI coding agents. (Source: JioHotstar Blog Post)

The filesystem baseline, which relied on locally checked out repositories and standard search and file operations, remained competitive on concrete tasks. Sourcebot, which provides indexed text search, symbol definitions, references, and file reads, performed better than the baseline on harder SWE-bench Verified tasks while also costing less. On simpler SWE-bench Lite tasks, retrieval generally added overhead without consistently improving results.

CodeScaleBench showed a different pattern. Semantic retrieval helped more when agents had to interpret ambiguous problem descriptions and map them to implementation details that were not obvious from exact text or symbol searches. The findings suggest that retrieval approaches should be selected according to task characteristics rather than treated as interchangeable solutions.

The report also highlighted the importance of tool design. Agents frequently preferred familiar developer operations such as searching text, reading files, and locating symbols over higher-level abstractions that required additional verification.

Tool call breakdown by category across coding agent knowledge base approaches. (Source: JioHotstar Blog Post)

Siddharth Vaithinathan raised a broader architectural question in a LinkedIn post discussing the study:

Whether coding agents should understand not only the code but also the company that produced it. He argued that repository indexing alone cannot capture why architectural decisions were made, which constraints shaped them, or what earlier incidents taught the engineering team.

Vaithinathan suggested extending agent knowledge beyond code and documentation to include architecture, constraints, decisions, rationale, incidents, and outcomes. Such context could help agents evaluate existing design choices before proposing changes, particularly in systems where historical operational experience influences architectural decisions.

Tarun Bhargava raises a relevant question for benchmark interpretation, particularly when evaluations use limited subsets and probabilistic models.

Cost/accuracy numbers with multiple runs of the same setup.

JioHotstar's evaluation did not identify a single retrieval approach that performed best across all tasks. Instead, JioHotstar recommends retaining filesystem tools as a baseline, using structural search for concrete, code-focused problems and semantic indexing for ambiguous or cross-cutting requirements. JioHotStar engineering team also emphasizes measuring tool-use traces alongside task accuracy to determine whether retrieval reduces unnecessary exploration. The findings highlight the importance of matching retrieval capabilities to the programming task and how the agent navigates the codebase.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness

#9821. Fine-tuning a 350M Model for Better Structured Outputs in 100 GRPO Steps

This guide is a fully public, inexpensive recipe for making a small model substantially better at structured-output compliance. We fine-tune LFM2.5-350M with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using the TRL library and evaluate it on the IFStruct benchmark. The full run takes around 500 samples and 100 training steps, small enough for a free-tier Colab or Kaggle GPU, and is available on GitHub. The results show that even a light fine-tuning procedure improves performance from 22.6% to 29.7% on the IFStruct benchmark.

Structured output is one of the most common real-world tasks for LLMs, yet most benchmarks fold it into broader reasoning or extraction scores rather than measuring it on its own. Whether a model reliably returns valid, parseable output in the requested format and shape — schema compliance — is often what decides whether it can be wired into a downstream system at all.

Note that the training pipeline described here is not the one used to train the RL model described in the IFStruct blog. This notebook doesn't aim to recreate the IFStruct benchmark score, but to show how task-specific fine-tuning of smaller models can improve performance and match that of far larger models.

This guide has two halves that run in different places:

We will need uv for the Python tooling and llama.cpp for serving. Following the Liquid AI llama.cpp deployment docs, install llama.cpp with Homebrew and verify that llama-server is available:

Before we begin, let's evaluate LFM2.5-350M on the IFStruct benchmark and see whether we can reproduce the reported score of 21.1%.

IFStruct is a benchmark for testing the validity of LLM outputs and schema adherence. The benchmark is open-source in Liquid4All/ifstruct, with the public benchmark dataset available on Hugging Face at LiquidAI/ifstruct-v1.0.

For the eval comparison, we serve the model locally on the MacBook with llama.cpp. We will use the BF16 GGUF (LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M-GGUF).

Then we start the base-model server with the following command:

Once the server is running, we can run the full benchmark with 2000 samples:

The IFStruct release blog reports 21.1% for LFM2.5-350M. Our local llama.cpp/BF16 setup measures 22.6%, close to the 21.1% reported in the IFStruct blog. We use this local result as the baseline for the same serving stack comparison.

The full, runnable pipeline lives in the accompanying notebook. We will cover only the relevant pieces in this section.

We use nvidia/Nemotron-RL-instruction_following-structured_outputs, which pairs each prompt with a target JSON Schema and an expected field count. We use about 500 samples for training.

Because the Nemotron data distribution differs from the IFStruct evaluation, we augment the prompts to close two gaps between them:

We load LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M and attach a LoRA adapter. Because LFM2.5 uses a hybrid attention/convolution architecture, we target the LFM-specific module names:

This trains ~6M parameters, about 1.66% of the model.

Then we define three reward functions, each on a [0, 1] scale, which score every completion on whether the extracted structure is correct:

We combine the three as a weighted sum with reward_weights=[1.0, 0.5, 2.0].

We train for 100 steps with 8 generations per prompt group, sized for a free-tier 16 GB GPU:

As you can see in the notebook, over the run, all three reward components climb, the KL from the reference model lifts off zero after warmup, and the truncated-completion fraction stays near zero.

Finally, we merge the LoRA adapter back into the base weights and save it as a single self-contained checkpoint, ready to convert to GGUF for serving:

After GRPO fine-tuning, we rerun the IFStruct evaluation. For this, we need to convert the merged model checkpoint into a BF16 GGUF. The converter script ships with the llama.cpp source, so we clone the repo once and install the converter's gguf package.

Then we serve the merged model with the following command:

Then, we will run the full IFStruct evaluation again with the fine-tuned model:

Comparing the two runs on the identical serving stack:

The gains land exactly where the training aimed: the JSON pass rate rises by nearly 14 points (18.0% → 31.9%), while YAML stays mostly the same. While this is still below the Qwen3.5-2B score of 33.15%, it shows that even light task-specific fine-tuning can bring a small model close to a larger one.

A short GRPO run with about 500 samples and 100 steps can lift a small 350M parameter model from 22.6% to 29.7% on IFStruct. The takeaway is that a cheap, task-specific reward signal can make a small model substantially more reliable about form, closing much of the gap to models several times its size.

To reproduce or extend this work, see the original IFStruct v1.0 blog post, the Liquid4All/ifstruct benchmark repo, and the LiquidAI/ifstruct-v1.0 dataset.

#9820. [$] Additional hardening for the glibc dynamic linker

The Node.js project recently had a security vulnerability that affected its Brotli decoder. The bug was a buffer overflow, but the particular way that official Node.js binaries are built for Linux meant that one of the main protections against turning a buffer overflow into remote code execution, address space layout randomization (ASLR) could not be turned on. If ASLR had been enabled, the bug would still be exploitable in theory, but much more difficult to exploit in practice. In response, the GNU C Library (glibc) is considering a new set of tunable settings to allow administrators to forbid programs that do not support ASLR. The new settings, while a welcome hardening measure, may not address the root problem.

#9819. Adapting CPython for yk

Earlier this year I wrote a post on yk, which can automatically add JIT compilers to C interpreters. Since then weâve applied yk to more interpreters, fixed various bugs, and improved performance notably. Towards the end of October I showed some data where on our benchmark suite1 yklua is 2Ã faster than the PUC Lua interpreter it takes as a base.

I was quite pleased with myself until someone brought me down to earth by asking âhow do you know if this works for large interpreters?â Itâs a fair question: PUC Lua is at least an order of magnitude smaller2 than CPython or CRuby and whoâs to say if it would work with much bigger interpreters? We had looked at CPython a year or so ago, but at that point yk was missing several obvious things that CPython would need, so we quickly moved on. A lot has changed since then, and a quick LLM experiment got far enough to suggest it would be worth looking again.

Happily, having taken a deeper look, CPython not only works when adapted for yk as ykcpython3, but there are meaningful performance gains to be had â not only relative to normal CPython, but also relative to Pythonâs experimental JIT4. Roughly speaking, this is the result of 3-4 daysâ work on ykcpython directly; there was a separate week and a half of generic yk bug fixing necessary to get to the point that I could look at ykcpython itself.

Here are the âfinalâ numbers from my brief odyssey on ykcpython and the AWFY benchmark suite:

In this table cpython is ânormalâ CPython 3.15.1; cpython_jit is CPython 3.15.1 with the experimental JIT turned on; and ykcpython is commit 31b4d387. Times are in seconds (lower is better) with means and 99% confidence intervals bootstrapped from 30 process executions, running on a 64 core AMD EPYC 7773X Debian machine in performance mode (download the repeatable experiment and the raw data). On each row the fastest entry(s) are shown in bold.

A simple summary of the table is: ykcpython is faster than cpython on every benchmark except DeltaBlue (where itâs about 2.5% slower); and faster than cpython_jit on 8 out of 13 benchmarks.

The point of this post is not to pretend that ykcpython is in any way ready for people to use â it definitely is not! Nor is it to pretend that one can expect performance on a wider set of programs to be as good as the numbers above â it definitely wonât! My view is that benchmark suite performance is a hoop to jump through rather than an end in itself: a system which benchmarks well might perform poorly in the real world; but a system which benchmarks poorly nearly always performs poorly in the real world.

Rather, I wanted to use this post as a way of showing what itâs like to adapt an interpreter for yk5: the stages I went through; and to give a sense of how the just under 450LoC I added were enough to achieve a meaningful effect. Luckily I had a sense that this might be a useful journey, so I was able to write enough stuff down to be able to flesh out this full post.

If you havenât read the earlier yk post, hereâs a very brief refresher. Given a lightly modified C interpreter6 as input, yk produces a VM with a meta-tracing JIT compiler as output7. yk doesnât aim to produce the fastest possible JIT compiling language implementation: rather, it aims to make the language implementation you know and love somewhat faster while retaining 100% compatibility. Put another way a âykifiedâ interpreter is a fork of the existing C version of the interpreter, with (hopefully!) a handful of adjustments.

As with any meta-tracing JIT compiler, yk identifies hot loops in the guest language (e.g. Lua or Python), and traces the interpreter (i.e. records what the C code is executing while it is interpreting the guest language). It then optimises those traces and converts them to machine code.

yk requires interpreters to tell it where potential loops in the guest language are via the YkLocation struct. Optionally â though if you want to get good performance, definitely necessary! â interpreter authors can add optimisation hints that embed knowledge about the language or its common idioms of use such as âat this point this seemingly dynamic value almost never changesâ. In general, working out where to put YkLocations is relatively easy, but working out where to put hints requires a much greater understanding of the interpreter, and careful measurement to understand which do and donât help.

The challenge I face when adapting an interpreter for yk is that I rarely know the interpreter well, if at all. Rather than trying to do everything at once, I have learnt to start off as simple as possible: I try and do the minimum changes that lead to some traces being recorded and compiled to machine code. This can be trickier than it seems: Iâve got to understand the build system8, and work out where to put some semi-sensible YkLocations. Iâve also learnt to make sure that the languageâs test suite works from this very first step: keeping it working thereafter is not only much easier, but it lessens the number of times one attempts optimisations that are unsound.

For a simple interpreter, you might get a basic JIT compiler from an interpreter with fewer than 10LoC (Lines-of-Code) changed. For somewhat bigger interpreters, a few more changes tend to be necessary. For example, yk doesnât like âthreadedâ interpreters that use goto between opcodes, because it doesnât give it enough opportunities to intercede and see whatâs going on. Fortunately, such changes are not generally too big.

Since it had been a long time since I looked at CPythonâs internals9, I started with the part I was vaguely familiar with. As I later discovered, this is now called the âtier 1â interpreter. Quickly hacking in support for yk highlighted several missing things in yk (from basic atomic loads to not-implemented-bit-widths in sub, minor incompatibilities (e.g. reading an environment variable after a CPython test had wiped it), and flat out bugs (from stackmap fixes to not doing silly things after fork). Fixing all those took me around a week and a half; Iâm not going to talk about them in detail in this post, because theyâre generic fixes that arenât ykcpython specific.

My adaption of the tier 1 interpreter is deliberately minimalistic. Most of the changes in the 200LoC diff are small one-offs that arenât hugely interesting: we need CPython to use its (builtin but non-default) switch-based interpreter; and yk uses a shadow stack, so CPythonâs C stack resizing needs to take that into account too. The most interesting thing I did was to add YkLocations at backwards jump opcodes, which I expected to be enough for some half-sensible traces to be created.

I wasnât expecting this first version of ykcpython to be faster than CPython â if nothing else, it contained almost no optimisation hints â but it was much slower than I expected. It was definitely creating traces, and they were executing correctly â the test suite passed, albeit taking more memory than Iâd like10 â but something clearly wasnât right.

Fortunately, it didnât take very long to work out what. 4 years ago, CPython added support for quickening under the heading of âspecialisationâ. Quickening is a simple, clever technique for improving interpreter performance that rewrites âgenericâ opcodes (e.g. âadd objectsâ) to âspecialisedâ, faster, opcodes (e.g. âadd two intsâ) when possible, deoptimising back to the generic opcodes if necessary. I tend to think of quickening as giving a decent portion of the benefit of a JIT compiler without all the bother of generating machine code11. The problem for yk is that sometimes a programâs opcodes can transition between specialised and unspecialised opcodes a large number of times, and the simple way Iâd added yk support meant that each transition implicitly threw away the associated trace and created a new one. In most cases, traces werenât used long enough to overcome the cost of creating them.

There are techniques which can overcome this problem, and I did briefly experiment with them, but I then recalled a conversation I had with some CPython developers last year. A quick look inside CPython confirmed my recollection: CPython contains a âtier 2â interpreter as well. This isnât a completely new interpreter; rather it is an alternative implementation of core parts of the main interpreter loop, mostly intended for CPythonâs experimental JIT compiler.

A very quick experiment later suggested that the tier 2 interpreter was â at least at a basic level â a better fit for yk12. I thus ripped out the tier 1 support and added support for yk in the tier 2 interpreter. Happily, tier 2 support is even easier than tier 1 support, consisting of a mere 80 LoC. To give you a quick idea of what yk support looks like, hereâs the part that attaches YkLocations13 to the (start of) loops:

For the rest of this post, Iâm going to be using yk and the tier 2 interpreter as the starting point for ykcpython.

When optimising any language implementation, itâs important to know where its performance sits in the wider performance landscape. To understand how ykcpython was doing, I used two other baselines: âstockâ CPython; and CPython with the experimental JIT. I configured cpython as follows:

Note that Iâm deliberately using the same version of LLVM for both cpython and cpython_jit because the latter requires LLVM-21. ykllvm â the fork of LLVM used in yk â is based off a version of LLVM about 6 months later than LLVM-21. That might slightly distort comparisons, but itâs a small enough difference that the effects hopefully are fairly minor. Bearing that in mind, ykcpython is configured as follows:

I used our fork14 of the AWFY benchmark suite, simply because I know how to run it without thinking.

The next challenge is to define a metric, or metrics, to report performance. Every metric has the potential to mislead and many are difficult to understand. In my opinion, the least worst single metric is wall-clock time: how long does my program take to run from start to finish? This doesnât capture everything we want to know, but it captures a lot, and itâs easy to understand.

Most importantly this metric implicitly includes start-up and warm-up time. In other words Iâm deliberately choosing a timing metric which tends to favour normal interpreters and âpenaliseâ JIT compilers. To somewhat offset that, we run each AWFY benchmark for 10 in-process iterations (i.e. run the whole benchmark in a for 0..10 loop) so that we also get some sense of how optimisation benefits longer-running programs.

The big performance table at the start of this post uses a custom benchmark runner on an idle machine. All the timings from now on in the post are from me running time once as a normal user without being too careful if the machine is completely idle or not: when starting to optimise an interpreter, itâs not practical to wait an hour to benchmark every change on many benchmarks, when the effects are generally quite large15.

There are various ways one can go about optimising an interpreter for meta-tracing, all of which have pros and cons: the sequence of optimisations Iâm showing here is just one way of going about things16.

Letâs start with the mandelbrot benchmark on cpython:

In other words, I ran the benchmark with 10 in-process iterations and a parameter of 500. The AWFY harness prints out how long each iteration took. As is common â but definitely not universal! â for an interpreter, cpython had fairly consistent times from one iteration to the next.

For this benchmark, cpython_jit takes 6.746s (0.58Ã CPython) and ykcpython takes a whopping 13.70s (1.17Ã CPython)17:

There are a couple of useful things to notice here. First, we can see warm-up occurring: ykcpythonâs first iteration is slower than subsequent iterations. Thatâs OK in my book: yk isnât really intended for programs running in a fraction of a second. Second, the 102% cpu and user time that is higher than wall-clock time are due to yk running trace compilation in threads. That allows the interpreter to continue executing, reducing perceived pauses.

The first thing I do in this situation is look at the âhigh-level IRâ (HIR) of the traces that yk has produced to see if things look sensible:

The logfile contains 11 traces, of which 1 is a âloopâ trace. In general, loop traces are where yk is most effective, and the non-loop traces are the price we have to pay to get the promised land of loop traces. In this case, a simple profile showed that most execution time is spent in the solitary loop trace, which is a promising start for yk.

At this point, doing much more with the HIR than this high-level analysis is difficult, because the output is 20,772 lines of this sort of thing:

Even if youâre used to this syntax and way of thinking, it can be incredibly hard to see the forest for the trees: thereâs just too much stuff. And that isnât just a problem for humans (or AIs) reading this: more HIR means more machine code which implies slower execution.

My first port of call when optimising an interpreter is to tackle interpreter dispatch. When an interpreter is executing a program, it continually asks âwhat is the opcode of the current instruction? Is it an add or a sub or â¦?â and then it dispatches to the code that performs the appropriate action. Itâs probable that a large chunk of that 20KLoC of HIR is the interpreter loading an opcode from memory and checking what kind it is. ykâs trace optimiser has various classic compiler tricks up its sleeve, but in this case they donât really help, because in most cases between the same instruction being loaded twice from memory, some other code will be called that yk has to assume might have mutated that memory. This isnât unnecessary conservatism: Python programs really can mutate their functionâs instructions!

I was particularly lucky because the tier2 interpreter uses âexecutorsâ which are traces of (optimised) instructions. Those instructions are immutable in the context of a given executor: should a Python functionâs instructions change, any associated executors will be invalidated. That means that we can attach a simple monotonically increasing integer code ID to a _PyExecutorObject and know that for a given code ID, an opcode at index I will always be the same.

This allows us to use the single most effective optimisation hint in yk: idempotent functions. In essence, an idempotent function says âfor the same inputs this function will always produce the same outputâ18. âAlwaysâ here really means âalwaysâ! Idempotent is a very strong guarantee that yk cannot help you uphold: if you fail to do so, your system will go wrong in weird ways.

Although yk provides a helper yk_idempotent_load function, we need something more specialised. Fortunately itâs not hard to write what we need:

Unsurprisingly, the yk_idempotent attribute tells yk that idempotent_load_opcode is an idempotent function. That means that if, in a particular trace, the function is called with parameters that are constant values then yk can remove the idempotent function call and replace it with its output. The __asm__ line is there to encourage LLVM not to inline the function19 (if the function is inlined, yk no longer knows there is anything idempotent there).

Using this requires changing just a few lines in the core interpreter loop. The most important lines are simply this:

Promotion (e.g. yk_promote)20 says âthis variable is expected to be semi-constant: record its concrete value and specialise the trace to it, but insert a guard in case that value later changesâ. Imagine I have yk_promote(x) and when a trace is later recorded, x happens to be 3. The trace will record guard true (x == 3): if on later runs x is not 3, the guard will fail and the trace will deoptimise; if the guard succeeds we know henceforth that x is definitely 3.

In other words, in the context of the traces weâre recording, yk will see calls to idempotent_load_opcode with constant arguments, allowing it to replace the function call with a constant result. The point of this isnât just to remove the cost of a load: rather, exposing constant data to ykâs trace optimiser allows it to do a much better job of optimising traces. The effect in this case is quite something:

In other words, that simple change has not only made ykcpython 2.7Ã faster, but it is now 0.43Ã cpython and 0.74Ã cpython_jit! In other words, a simple PR that changes 30LoC has made this benchmark over twice as fast as CPython and 25% faster than CPythonâs JIT. Another way of judging the effectiveness of this optimisation is that it has reduced the 20,772 lines of HIR output to 7,648 lines21.

However, before we get carried away, this isnât enough to make all benchmarks magically quicker. I have learnt from experience to rotate between benchmarks to avoid over-training22. In this case I decided to look at the deltablue benchmark, which I know from yklua can be a tough target. The situation in ykcpython turned out to be worse than I expected: cpython takes 7.67s, cpython_jit takes 6.20s, and ykcpython (with our idempotent change) takes 37.51s. Ouch!

My next port of call is to run YKD_LOG=2 which prints warnings if a trace canât be compiled. Sure enough:

For now Iâm going to skip âtrace too longâ. In essence yk has a fixed limit for âthis trace looks to be so long that itâs probably not usefulâ. The limit was too low, so I increased it unilaterally before doing the work for this post. Exactly what the right value is I donât know. Indeed, I think that this crude heuristic probably needs replacing with something more sophisticated: doing that is a problem for another day.

Letâs move onto the âunimplementedâ warning: I havenât got around to implementing complex atomic instructions yet, so as soon as one of those is encountered, yk has no choice but to give up on that trace entirely. If it happens to be a hot part of a benchmark, that can absolutely kill performance. In this case, happily, the atomicrmw warnings just so happened to come from functions which we really donât want to inline into the trace anyway.

One of tracingâs virtues is that it aggressively inlines functions, but that can inline checks which fail too often on subsequent executions. For example, one function we inline by default is _PyObject_GC_Link which checks to see if enough objects have been allocated for garbage collection to be worth scheduling. If weâre unlucky, we may trace an iteration of a loop which happens to schedule garbage collection: in nearly every subsequent execution, the resulting guard will fail, and weâll take a somewhat slower path. The solution here is to mark such functions as yk_outline:

Functions marked yk_outline become calls in a trace. There are probably a number of functions which should be marked as yk_outline, but I marked the two that happened to cause the aborted warnings and that also obviously we donât want to include in a trace anyway. Doing so improved execution time to 36.63s (about 2.5% faster), so theyâre clearly not the major cause of the slowdown in this case.

Just when I was starting to fret, profiling execution showed that, to my surprise, deltablue was only spending about half its running time in JIT-compiled code, where one would expect it to be spending 90%+. It turns out that the main reason for this is that not all executors have a _JUMP_TO_TOP opcode and werenât being traced.

My quick fix was to add a YkLocation at the first opcode in an executor. The one line fix does just that: it means that yk starts tracing as soon as it enters an executor. Doing so improves deltablueâs execution time to 8.64s (4.23Ã faster than before). Thatâs still 1.13Ã CPython, but itâs a lot better than before!

At the time I made this change I didnât fully think about how adding a YkLocation at the start of an executor might interact with the YkLocation already added to _JUMP_TO_TOP. As luck would have it, I accidentally stumbled on a reasonable combination: _JUMP_TO_TOP tends to jump to the instruction at index 1. Still, I suspect that there might be a better way to add YkLocations to executors, but one canât solve every problem all at once: itâs time to move onto the next thing!

Our earlier use of idempotent loads made such a huge impact on interpreter dispatch that itâs easy to overlook that it was a simple, shallow, change: it only optimised loading an instructionâs opcode kind. Instructions contain a number of other fields that are equally amenable to idempotent loading.

There are various ways one can go about optimising these additional fields. I could, for example, have replaced the definitions of some static functions in header files. To keep things simple, I defined a macro which can generate the two-parameter functions we need, and then nobbled some other macros to call it at appropriate points. With the resulting change deltablueâs performance improves to 8.09s â weâre now within 10% of cpythonâs performance.

As we saw earlier, not all functions are good candidates for inlining into a trace. yk has a very simple heuristic â stolen shamelessly from RPython/PyPy â which is to mark functions containing loops as âoutlinedâ. In other words, if C calls a function f() and f contains for (...) { ... } then yk will not inline calls to f.

The fundamental reason not to inline functions-with-loops is that tracing unrolls loops, and that tends not to be a good idea. First, some loops execute vast numbers of iterations, which would cause counter-productively-long traces. Second, loopsâ iterations are often controlled by dynamic, ever-changing values: unrolling would specialise the trace to just one of those values, giving suboptimal performance on every other value.

There are however a small number of functions in an interpreter which we actively want to unroll. Typically those functionsâ loops satisfy two properties: they only run a small number of iterations; and the number of iterations depends on an aspect of the userâs program that changes rarely. For example, a function called unpack_args(int num_args) which contains for (int i=0; i

yk thus provides a yk_unroll attribute, which informs yk that a function that might otherwise be outlined should in fact be inlined and its loops unrolled. Rather than slog through every function in CPython looking for candidates, I did a simple grep/sort in hir to see which (implicitly non-inlined) C functions appear most often in traces23:

bcmp is the standard libc function: all of the other functions are in CPython itself. Not all of those functions will have loops in them, but the chances are that most do. What I do in such a situation is go down (or, depending how you look at it, up) the list and look at the code in each function. I did that for a couple of benchmarks to ensure I got some coverage of common functions.

The two most commonly called CPython functions immediately looked like good candidates. _PyFrame_Initialize is the most obvious of the two, containing almost exactly the pattern I most like to match on:

_PyFrame_ClearLocals is slightly trickier: it contains a while loop involving pointer arithmetic, but it didnât take me long to convince myself that it was a good candidate.

Earlier we made _PyObject_GC_Link not inlineable, so we donât want to reverse that! Similarly, do_lookup looks values up in a dictionary, so we want to keep that outlined: it depends on an often-changing dynamic value.

PyLong_FromSsize_t and PyLong_FromLong were harder to judge. These functionsâ inner loops depend on dynamic values, but my best guess is that they tend to be fairly stable in practice. I will be keeping an eye on these functions in the future, because I only have medium confidence that I made the right initial call.

As these examples suggest, I am generally fairly cautious about adding yk_unroll: inappropriate placings can easily help one benchmark and make many others worse. I thus tend to only mark one or two functions as yk_unroll, benchmark, and then move on. In this case, I did 5 small PRs, with the end effect that json went from 11.52s to 10.85s.

In general most function calls in C are direct: f() calls a function called f. However a minority of functions are indirect: f is a generic pointer whose value can be any compatible function. This is commonly used in interpreters to allow run-time dispatch to type specific code.

By default, yk cannot inline through indirect function calls, because without knowing exactly what pointer is being called, it canât reliably reconstruct the path that execution took24. Fortunately, we already have the tool we need to solve this problem: yk_promote! If yk sees an indirect function call with a constant pointer it knows exactly what function is being called and can inline as normal. The common pattern I use is:

yk_is_interpreting() is true during ânormalâ interpretation; false during tracing; and (because itâs a constant false) removed during tracing. In other words, yk_promote is only called during the tracing phase. yk_is_interpreting() is fairly fast (much faster than yk_promote()) so this idiom is a small but useful performance win.

However, there is often a second problem. yk only puts the tracing machinery into a function if it can statically prove that it is reachable from a traceable path. Commonly, functions called from indirect calls cannot be statically proven to be traceable and thus they still leave an outlined call in the trace. We can solve that with the yk_indirect_inline function which tells yk âthis function can be reached from an indirect call and should be considered for tracingâ25.

Profiling a couple of benchmarks quickly showed several potential candidates26. My experience is that not all indirect call sites are good targets for promotion: for example, of the interpreters Iâve looked at so far, inlining malloc and free indirect calls has rarely been profitable. However, I quickly alighted upon a couple of promising candidates.

Letâs start with the less promising, but easier to explain, one: benchmarks like deltablue and json call len on lists and strings. Simplifying slightly, sq_length is a pointer to a function inside a CPython type, so this becomes an indirect call in traces. In the case of len([...]) the function thatâs ultimately called is list_length:

where PyList_GET_SIZE boils down (slightly elided) to a simple load a->ob_size. Thatâs the sort of code that yk loves to see inlined in a trace!

The resulting PR has to do a slightly annoying dance to make yk accept the yk_promote call. In essence, if yk_promote were to be statically inlined into a function which ykllvm determines doesnât need to be traced, odd things happen, and so ykllvm throws a static error. In this case, the function that âshouldâ contain the yk_promote can get inlined in multiple paths, one of which falls foul of this check. A hacky fix is to pull the promote out into a function which isnât statically inlined27. I then did a second PR to inline range construction and iteration.

You may notice that in both of these PRs I have marked a much larger number of functions yk_indirect_inline than I have benchmark evidence for. The reason for this is a variant of something I mentioned above: my experience of indirect call sites is that either nearly all targets benefit from indirect inlining or none do. This clearly isnât an iron law of the universe, but what it means is that I tend to look at all the possible targets, and mark them as yk_indirect_inline if they look sensible. So far, I have rarely regretted doing so.

Collectively these two PRs drive jsonâs performance down to 10.41s, though the effect on deltablue was too small to say anything either way. As I get further into optimising an interpreter for yk this is common: not all benchmarks benefit from all optimisations.

At this point, youâve probably got a good sense of how I approach ykifying an interpreter. I raised a few more PRs before realising that I wasnât going to add much useful conceptually to this post: it was time to finish this stage of work off and write it up.

Before I started this little journey, I wasnât entirely sure if yk would work at all â let alone âwellâ! â on an interpreter the size and complexity of CPython. The early stages didnât entirely dispel my worries: there were lots of missing pieces, and quite a few bugs, that needed fixing in yk for ykcpython to work at all. The fact that ykcpython does work, and works fairly well, is proof that at least one big, complex, interpreter can be ykified with relative ease â and that it can be surprisingly competitive on performance.

Of course, I am lucky in many ways. yk already had decent foundations, thanks to several peopleâs hard work. The tier 2 interpreter in CPython made my life a lot easier than it might otherwise have been. Small benchmarks, like the ones Iâve used in this post, tend to flatter (meta-)tracing as a JIT compiling technique. And when it comes to ykifying interpreters, well, Iâve been round the block a few times.

But I donât want to completely underplay things. 3-4 days isnât that long to spend on an interpreter like CPython. It will take a lot longer than that â even with the wonder of LLMs to speed up the journey â to do a thorough job and squeeze all the juice that ykcpython can expose to yk. Similarly, I have only looked at a handful of benchmarks: itâs unlikely that ykcpython will magically speed up a wide range of programs yet, as there will be many other parts of CPython that need to be considered for optimisation. A lot of this will not be rocket science, but it is work, and not all of it can yet be automated.

I also havenât made any performance optimisations (yet!) to yk for ykcpython specifically (though I have fixed a couple of bottlenecks that I had previously been able to ignore). In particular, one thing I am entirely confident in is that ykcpython will generate HIR patterns that yk doesnât yet optimise effectively: fixing those will improve ykcpythonâs performance for free, possibly quite a bit. Even without that, ykcpython has highlighted additional bottlenecks in yk that had never previously been an issue: each time one of those is fixed, ykcpython will magically get faster.

In a sense, this is one of the nice things that yk offers: improvements to yk nearly always benefit every ykified interpreter. Itâs why I could bring ykcpython up to speed in a short period of time: I wasnât writing a JIT compiler from scratch, I was reusing a generic toolkit. For example, the various missing pieces and bugs that ykcpython highlighted in yk will almost certainly make ykifying the next interpreter that bit easier â and hopefully future improvements to yk will benefit ykcpython even further!

Acknowledgments: Edd Barrett and Lukas Diekmann did much of the original work on yk. Shopify and the Royal Academy of Engineering generously funded the underlying research. Chris Seaton was the person who made the work on yk possible.

#9818. Why Europe's Freezer Hacks Spread So Far, So Fast

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Europe's supermarket freezer hacks show how security issues can cascade across an industry, disrupting supply chains at scale.

The recent refrigerator hacks wreaking havoc across European supermarkets is a lesson in how shared weaknesses in operational technology (OT) can spread across a whole supply chain.

On the night of Oct. 11, an attacker reportedly compromised refrigeration controls used by hundreds of French supermarkets, triggering extended defrost cycles in refrigerators and freezers across the country. The incident caused millions of euros in damage across roughly 700 affected stores in France alone, spoiling food, damaging equipment, and even reportedly starting some fires in the process.

The technology leveraged in these attacks included Danfoss refrigeration controllers, as well as Dixell and Copeland XWEB systems. It's unclear how the threat actor gained access to these systems.

However, the Danfoss controllers at the center of this campaign ran Internet-accessible Web servers. Many were accessible using default login credentials: "admin" as the username and the current date as the password. CERT-FR made a number of recommendations in an advisory to affected supermarkets, such as changing default passwords, factory resetting compromised equipment, and updating firmware. Though to that last point, Danfoss told AFP that many of the attacks involved legacy products that no longer receive updates.

Related:Les supermarchés de l'UE paient d'un firmware de réfrigérateur non mis à jour

France's Cyber Crisis Coordination Center (C4) on Nov. 9 published a five page report attributing the series of attacks on Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), and specifically on the IRGC's Shahid Shoostari and Shahid Kaveh cyber-offensive units.

France's Ministry of Europe and Foreign Affairs said in a statement that the country will propose to its European partners new sanctions against the Iranian entities and individuals allegedly involved in the cyberattack, adding that France reserves the right to take additional proportionate measures to respond to the attacks.

What stands out about the French supermarket attacks is how a shared weakness in refrigeration infrastructure appears to have enabled disruption across hundreds of stores. While investigators have not publicly confirmed the initial access vector, the incident raises questions about the risks created when organizations rely on similar technologies, deployment models, and remote-access practices.

Chris St. Myers, director of SentinelLABS, says evidence suggests a common exposure problem, rather than market concentration, may have facilitated this issue.

"CERT-FR confirmed that the French compromises involved Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC controllers, along with Copeland and Dixell XWEB systems. These technologies are deployed across many retail environments, often with similar remote access requirements and configurations," St. Meyers says. "That creates opportunities for attackers to reuse the same techniques across otherwise unrelated organizations."

Related:EU Grocers Pay a Steep Price for Unpatched Fridge Firmware

Thomas Plank, CEO of industrial security firm Tributech, similarly diagnosed common exposure as a core issue behind the attacks.

"What's concentrated is the setup. Across chains and countries, it's the same model: remote-management controllers reachable from the internet, often on out-of-support firmware, maintained by a small number of contractors who look after hundreds of stores from one place," Plank tells Dark Reading. "When everyone runs the same risky pattern through the same few channels, one way in reaches many retailers at once, across borders, overnight. That's why this looks like a campaign rather than a string of unlucky stores."

It's highly unusual and hardly precedented for a cyberattack to have such a significant impact on the food supply chain, but it's not the only incident like it in recent memory.

A similar attack hit refrigeration and freezer systems in stores across other countries at the beginning of November, including Belgium, Estonia, Germany, Ireland, Luxembourg, Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Spain, and Sweden. Around the same time, attackers targeted the refrigeration of three blood banks operated by the national French Blood Establishment, though the attack was stopped before blood plasma was damaged.

Related:Taiwan Bullet Train Hack Highlights Cybersecurity Gaps in Rail Systems

For as alarming and impactful these incidents may seem, supply chain targeting has become more common in recent years with 2021's Colonial Pipeline attack, Iran's recent targeting of fuel monitoring systems around the US, and 2024's Change Healthcare incident.

The danger is clear, especially in the context of a supermarket. Piotr Buliński, chief technology officer (CTO) of Internet of Things (IoT) device management firm Qbee, says a supermarket chain runs thousands of small, unattended OT systems between refrigeration, HVAC, and building management. "Each one is 'just a few controllers,' so nobody treats them as critical infrastructure," he says. "Yet when they fail, the damage is immediate and physical."

These incidents remind us once again about the importance of securing critical infrastructure.

Updating OT systems is a challenging task in their own right because of the downtime often required. Much of the critical technology holding up industrial processes is intended to operate for years (if not decades) on end, while the organizations relying on OT can often include those too under-resourced to have dedicated security staff, like municipalities, or indeed, supermarkets.

Even as these problems have gotten a little easier to address over the years and many dedicated firms have risen to address these challenges, organizations still struggle to secure OT.

St. Meyers believes retail OT has historically received less security attention than traditional industrial environments, despite carrying many of the same underlying risks. He says this is possibly in part because refrigeration, HVAC, and building management systems are "often deployed and maintained outside the traditional IT security organization," despite being OT.

Plank agrees. He says one solution for retailers is to verify commands at the device level against engineering limits, as "no freezer should ever accept a command to go to 50°C, whoever sends it and whatever channel it arrives on," referencing the extreme temperatures some targeted equipment reached during the attacks.

For organizations outside the sphere of influence that want to learn from what happened here, there are several lessons: Don't use default passwords, take inventory of where and how industrial technologies are internet accessible, remove internet exposure wherever possible, and make sure all points of access are secured.

Rafe Pilling, senior director of threat research at Sophos, tells Dark Reading that generally, this incident should be seen as a warning to retailers. "Industrial systems, from energy production to water management to food refrigeration, must be secured," he says, "and at a minimum not accessible to malicious hackers via the Internet."

This story was updated at 2:20 p.m. ET on Nov. 9 to reflect France's accusations against Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

Alex is an award-winning writer, journalist, and podcast host based in Boston. After cutting his teeth writing for independent gaming publications as a teenager, he graduated from Emerson College in 2016 with a Bachelor of Science in journalism. He has previously been published on VentureFizz, Search Security, Nintendo World Report, and elsewhere.

At Dark Reading, he covers a variety of cybersecurity topics, including the cybercrime ecosystem, open source security, and the intersection between AI and threat actors. In his spare time, Alex hosts the weekly Nintendo podcast, "Talk Nintendo Podcast," and works on personal writing projects, including two previously self-published science fiction novels.

He has received numerous awards, including TechTarget's Writer of the Year in 2022 as well as more than 10 Azbee awards for his reporting between 2022 and today.

#9817. In Memoriam: Tim Peters 1952–2026

It's hard to overestimate Tim's influence on Python. He's probably best known for writing the Zen of Python (PEP 20), but to me he was a mentor and language co-designer long before that. Tim found Python not long after its initial release. His first deed was to convince me that Python should support mixed arithmetic between int and float, because most users would expect them to work that way. And he never stopped contributing.
