#9800. tokenizers v1: encode, decode and scaling, measured

The tokenizer has not historically been the bottleneck within ML workflows. Compute-wise, tokenization is light compared to the heavy modeling happening in the rest of the pipeline. Yet, in some cases, it has rapidly become key to accelerating (or slowing down) your machine learning work.

As models become faster and workloads scale, that balance begins to shift. Training on massive datasets, serving many concurrent requests, or repeatedly processing long inputs can put enough pressure on the tokenizer that it starves the model of data.

This is why we have chosen to heavily focus on performance for the upcoming version 1 of tokenizers. Tokenization should be light and should scale with your workflow. Your GPUs should never sit idle waiting for the CPU to complete its tokenization.

In this article, we look at what makes v1 faster than v0.23, often by tens of times.

This work was entirely possible thanks to the rest of the ecosystem. Tokenization is a very active area of open source work, and libraries such as gigatoken, tiktoken, kitoken, tokie, fastokens, wordchipper and ai-tokenizer, as well as many others, have each pushed on what a fast tokenizer can be. We read that work, and several of the ideas below reached us because another project showed they were worth trying.

Before this refactor, tokenizers was nowhere near the performance it could have had, so contributing to it may not have seemed worth it. With this refactor, we hope to make clear that we intend tokenizers to be a library worth contributing to.

We also thank IBM, NVIDIA, and the ExecuTorch team for contributing patches and helping us test across a wide range of hardware to broaden platform support.

We showcase results for the release candidate of tokenizers v1 against other widely used alternatives. We go over single-threaded, multi-threaded, scaling across threads, per-model comparison, per-language comparison, latency, decoding throughput, memory heap, as well as crate size.

We run this from the tokbench repository, and add a command to rerun the benchmarks on your hardware if you would like to do so.

v1 will produce the same token IDs as v0.23. The goal was to preserve the output, the API, the vocabulary and the merge ranks, and improve everything that can be improved. That includes breadth. The library stays general across tokenizer families rather than specialising on BPE, so v1 loads everything v0.23 loaded.

A tokenizer converts text into the list of integers a model reads. tokenizers runs that conversion in four stages. Normalization applies operations such as lowercasing or Unicode normalization to the raw text. Pre-tokenization splits the text into smaller pieces called pre-tokens. The model turns each pre-token into tokens and maps them to IDs in its vocabulary. Post-processing adds any special tokens the model expects.

The model stage is where most of the work described here happens. Eight of the ten model families measured in this article use byte pair encoding, or BPE. BPE starts from the bytes of a pre-token and repeatedly joins the highest ranked adjacent pair until no ranked pair remains. The ranking is learned when the tokenizer is trained and ships with it, so the same text always produces the same IDs. A merge never crosses a pre-token boundary. The other two families use WordPiece and Unigram, the two other model types the library supports.

The tokenization pipeline page documents the four stages. Tokenization algorithms documents BPE, WordPiece and Unigram.

Each stage was worked on. These are the changes that mattered:

BPE models use a regular expression to split the input text into smaller, easier to process chunks called pre-tokens. Merges happen inside a pre-token and never across the boundary between two of them, so this split decides what the rest of the pipeline sees.

That regular expression is a fixed parameter of the model. It ships with the tokenizer and never changes at runtime, so there is no need for a general-purpose regex engine to interpret it on every encode. An equivalent splitting function can be written by hand, once, for the pattern a given model actually uses.

A hand-written function can then use the SIMD instructions (single instruction, multiple data) of a modern CPU, which apply one operation to many bytes at once and suit UTF-8 text well. bitcannon views the input's bytes as parallel streams of bits, so boundaries fall out of boolean operations across whole registers instead of a scan that advances one character at a time. It decides 64 bytes per register operation. The same idea drives Parabix for text processing and simdjson for JSON.

This depends on recognising the pattern. A handful of grammars cover most byte-level BPE models, and a tokenizer whose pattern is not among them keeps the regex path and none of this speed-up. That is why the gains above vary as much as they do.

Real text contains many repeated words. Because BPE always produces the same token IDs for a given pre-token, v1 can save the result after processing it once. A thread-local cache maps each pre-token's bytes to its token IDs, allowing later occurrences to skip the merge process.

Naturally, as the input grows, the number of unique words can grow more slowly than the total number of words. Repeated words then account for an increasing share of the input. New words still appear, which accounts for the occasional misses in the animation below.

Caching works best when the input contains repeated pre-tokens. Input with few repeated pre-tokens can pay for lookups without receiving many hits.

The next major cost comes from the BPE merge loop. For each pre-token, the loop repeatedly finds the highest-priority adjacent pair and merges it. The previous implementation allocated new memory for every call and built a new priority queue for every pre-token.

v1 reuses a scratch buffer owned by the caller, removing those repeated allocations. It stores symbols in a flat array and links adjacent symbols by their positions in that array, which makes updates during merging cheaper. It also processes a batch of pre-tokens in a single model call.

Each candidate pair is also packed into a single 64-bit value, with the merge rank in the high bits. Comparing two candidates is then just comparing two integers, and "no merge here" is the largest possible value, so the loop finds its next merge without a branch.

Small differences in benchmark design can produce large differences in tokenizer performance. We used the following rules to keep the comparison consistent across engines.

Repeatedly encoding one document can be faster than encoding a stream of distinct documents on the same build. The first approach measures performance when the entire document is already represented in the cache. The second measures performance on new input while allowing previously seen pre-tokens to remain cached.

Both conditions are sometimes described as "warm," even though they measure different workloads. Our headline results use distinct documents, and the complete corpus is too large to fit in the cache. Tokenizer benchmarks should identify which workload they use because the choice can dominate the result.

Across the ten model families v1's encode path covers, it encodes text 3 to 30 times faster than v0.23 with one thread on an Apple M4 Max. The low end is t5-base, the high end gpt2. It scales at 76% of linear across eight workers. Throughout these changes, v1 produces exactly the same token IDs as the released library.

The overall improvement comes from several changes working together: a hand-written splitter in place of a regex engine, a cache that answers a repeated word without merging it again, a merge loop that never touches the allocator, and one model call per batch of pre-tokens instead of one per pre-token. Each reduces the work done at a different point in the pipeline.

The next priority is support for more model families. We will move additional models onto the new merge loop before 1.0.0. Once the release candidates stabilize, the next step will be bringing about the improvements within the transformers library and the rest of the ecosystem which depend on the tokenizers library.

This post is generated from tokbench results and will be updated as support expands.

A release candidate for v1 is on crates.io. The API you call is the one you already call, so the only thing that changes is which build you install.

Training is behind a default-on feature that pulls a C++ dependency with it. If you only need to encode, turn it off to exclude the training implementation:

Encoding is unchanged: same call, same ids.

Every figure in this post was measured against this crate. The Python bindings wrap the same code and are built from bindings/python, but they add per-call overhead that none of these measurements include.

The benchmarks in this post cover the completed release-candidate work listed first. The remaining sections show what is still required for 1.0.0 and what we plan to explore afterward.

This work is in the Rust pre-release on crates.io:

Will have to try it out. Data seems real good.

#9799. Attackers Crash Claude's 'Office Party' Flaw to Run Malicious Code on Linux

Attackers can exploit a flaw in Claude's document-processing tool by creating a temporary file that Anthropic's AI assistant can access and run on a user's machine.

An attacker can use a flaw in Anthropic Claude's document-processing tool to run malicious code on Linux systems just by creating a temporary file that the AI assistant can access. The flaw highlights a growing risk posed by even trusted AI tools to introduce security gaps in enterprise environments.

Researchers from AIR Security discovered the flaw, which they've dubbed "Office Party," in Anthropic's official DOCX, PPTX, and XLSX skills, which are tools that enable Claude to create, read, edit, and process Microsoft Word documents, PowerPoint presentations, and Excel spreadsheets, respectively.

The vulnerability stems from a helper script, soffice.py, that launches LibreOffice to convert documents, including rendering Word documents as PDFs, they revealed in a report published today. When the script encounters an environment where Unix-domain sockets cannot be opened, it uses a workaround that loads a shared library through the Linux LD_PRELOAD mechanism.

Related:N-able Takes N-central Platform Offline After Discovery of 33 Flaws

Anthropic has opted not to fix the issue.

During conversation, the script checks whether a library named lo_socket_shim.so already exists in a shared temporary directory but does not verify its origin or contents. An attacker who can place a malicious library at that location before the next document-processing operation can potentially have their code loaded and executed within LibreOffice, with the privileges of the user running the AI agent.

In this way, the flaw can allow attackers to execute malicious code on a user's Linux machine by exploiting an unverified file path used during document conversion, explains Niv Hoffman, co-founder and chief technology officer (CTO) of AIR Research Lab, in an email interview.

"An attacker gets one malicious file into a shared temporary folder which many programs use, and the next time an employee asks Claude for a document, Anthropic's trusted skill loads that file and runs it," he tells Dark Reading.

The vulnerability affects Linux environments where Unix sockets are blocked, including certain container security configurations, and Claude Code's sandbox. AIR Security reports that macOS is not affected because it does not load the library through LD_PRELOAD.

The AIR researchers demonstrated two ways the attack can work on Linux systems. In one scenario, they manually placed a malicious library in the temporary directory before asking Claude Code to generate a document. In another, they used a separate, seemingly legitimate AI skill to unpack a supporting file into the same directory. When the document-processing skill subsequently ran, the malicious library was loaded automatically.

Related:Google, Partners Disrupt 1.3 Million-Device-Strong XCPE Botnet

The flaw presents a serious issue for enterprises running Linux because it exploits "the default skills that all Claude agents use — [of which there are] hundreds of millions — and one planted file can make them run an attacker’s code with the employee's own access," Hoffman explains.

This second attack scenario is particularly concerning for enterprise security teams because it illustrates how individually benign-looking AI skills can interact to create an attack chain. And often, "companies don't have visibility to which skills and other agent add-ons they have installed, and don't have a red button to revoke or patch a vulnerable one," Hoffman explains.

Moreover, a malicious or compromised skill does not necessarily need to exploit the document-processing tool directly; it may simply need to place a file that another trusted component will execute, according to the AIR researchers.

The AIR team discovered the flaw in May and reported it to Anthropic, which acknowledged its existence, according to the report. However, the AI company "considers it outside its security boundary, since the vulnerable code only runs inside a sandbox," AIR Research Lab's Omri Saxena and Or Nevo wrote in the report. This means that as of now, the helper script still uses the same fixed path and still loads whatever file it finds there, they said.

Related:'Aokigahara' Stealer Targets 'Developer Keyrings' & AI Assistants

Hoffman says that Anthropic's response is "not quite" adequate, "because even if the skills run within a sandbox, the attacker’s code then runs inside it with the user's own permissions, where the user's files and work already are," he says. Anthropic did not immediately return Dark Reading's request for comment about whether the company would take any further action to remedy the issue.

For businesses deploying AI agents and coding assistants, Office Party reinforces the need to treat AI skills as software dependencies rather than trusted extensions, and secure them as such, according to AIR.

To mitigate, organizations should make it a point to know "exactly what skills or add-ons an organization is using with Claude Code by keeping a live inventory of every AI skill and add-on across employees' agents," Hoffman says. They also should "review even official ones like any other code, and update or patch the whole set whenever a new vulnerability is published."

During her long career, Elizabeth has lived and worked as a full-time journalist in Phoenix, San Francisco, and New York City. She specializes in news coverage and analysis, using her years of experience to look at the current state of cybersecurity with a critical gaze. She currently resides in a village on the southwest coast of Portugal, where in her free time she enjoys surfing, hiking with her dogs, growing plants, and playing and performing as a singer and musician.

InfoQ Homepage News LinkedIn Replaces Argo CD with a Custom GitOps Engine for Kubernetes Deployments

Nov 12, 2026 4 min read

In a recent post, LinkedIn revealed it has replaced Argo CD with its own GitOps engine. This new system deploys applications across over 250 Kubernetes clusters. It supports more than 4,000 services and manages over 100,000 deployments each week. According to a post, deployment infrastructure failures fell from 925 to 63 despite a 3.7x increase in deployment volume. The median time to detect and conclude a failed deployment dropped from 16.1 to 2.45 minutes.

LinkedIn started with one Argo CD instance per cluster, a topology it chose because Argo CD already managed its cluster add-ons that way. Clusters run up to 5,000 nodes each. A central deployment orchestrator spawned an ephemeral pod per deployment, with Argo CD hidden behind it. The team lists seven problems that emerged at scale. Argo CD doesn't have an observedGeneration, so you can't link sync and health status to a specific deployment. LinkedIn created a Lua health check that uses a tracking annotation to address this. A Synced and Healthy application could also resolve to an unintended revision when stale repo-server cache entries were used.

Two of the issues were architectural. Argo CD maintains one watch per group-version-resource across Applications. LinkedIn’s clusters have low resource-type diversity. This means etcd churn from one app can slow syncs for all apps. In one test, sync took under 3 minutes on a cluster with 60,000 pods and over 10 minutes with more than 80,000. The second was server-side-apply PATCH. Kubernetes truncates managedFields once an object has had more than 10 distinct field managers, and the API server then forgets who owns a field. In LinkedIn's AI workloads, which run multiple containers per Pod, a container removed from a manifest could therefore survive on the live Pod. The team had pruning disabled because destructive operations in production require approval. The remaining problems were CRD schema changes that required controller restarts across the fleet. Some OutOfSync states did not reflect real drift. Error messages were buried in boilerplate.

LinkedIn evaluated Flux but found it shared the same controller paradigm, so it built the engine as a library. Each deployment runs in its pod, with no shared controller state. Updates use PUT for full replacements, not PATCH. They retry on resourceVersion conflicts with exponential backoff. A 3-way diff across the live object, the previously deployed manifest, and the newly rendered manifest detects drift, and genuine drift fails the deployment. The same pod then watches the object's status until it converges or times out, and the API server unwraps errors for the user. Objects missing from the rendered manifest become deletion candidates, subject to delete protection, and convergence logic for LinkedIn's CRDs is built in.

The comparison uses the same calendar month a year apart. The migration ran from July 2025 to April 2026, which makes May 2026 the first clean post-migration month. The infra failure count covers only failures caused by the deployment system and excludes drift errors, since the two systems define drift differently. LinkedIn states that the improvement isn't solely due to the new engine. The orchestrator's error classification and reliability also got better during this time. The median duration for successful deployments is similar for both systems. However, the mean and tail have improved. The team attributes this to a namespace-scoped informer cache.

The engine is internal, and no open-source release is mentioned. Argo CD remains in use at LinkedIn for cluster add-ons and system services. The team had also found that maintaining 200+ Argo CD instances made each upgrade a multi-week project.

Teams running Argo CD at scale can check two things without a rewrite. Count the field managers on long-lived objects, since managedFields truncation can leave orphaned containers that produce no error. Then check whether sync latency tracks total pod count on shared clusters, which points to watch contention. LinkedIn concludes that the build-or-extend decision relies on the operational model. They say that per-deployment isolation, not controller tuning, allows the system to scale with compute.

LinkedIn is not the only large operator to build deployment logic around Kubernetes rather than adopt a general-purpose GitOps controller. Uber’s Up platform assigns each deployment to a dedicated controller. This is the Uber Deployment Controller. It translates the intent into Kubernetes primitives and sends status updates. This helps the workflow move forward. Uber keeps a long-running controller, while LinkedIn runs one ephemeral pod per deployment with no shared controller state.

Airbnb went further back and built its own tooling years earlier. In a talk at QCon London 2019 on InfoQ, infrastructure engineer Melanie Cebula introduced kube-gen. This internal framework creates Kubernetes configuration from one versioned project file. It also includes a deploy tool that applies or replaces objects and restarts pods, so changes take effect right away. Airbnb's deploy tool also returns an atomic success or failure, and a container that restarts for 30 seconds at the start of a rollout counts as a failed deploy. Airbnb was then at roughly 125,000 production deploys a year.

#9797. Introducing Polo: a Wayland MATE compositor

Kerem Söke has announced the 1.0 release of Polo, a Wayland compositor for the MATE Desktop Environment:

The idea is to keep MATE behaving as closely as possible to how it does on X11, rather than changing the desktop to fit a different compositor. [...]

Window management, metacity, workspaces, tiling, XWayland, clipboard and clipman support, multiple monitors, display scaling, hotplugging, screenshots, screen sharing, and session management are all working.

I've also added desktop effects: fade, zoom, zap, spin, squeemize, magic lamp, desktop cube, expo, and wobbly windows.

Söke is looking for people to test Polo, particularly on multi-monitor setups, and report back with problems.

#9796. Black Hat India 2026 Makes a Landmark Debut in Bengaluru, Bringing the Global Cybersecurity Community to India

Inaugural edition by Informa Markets in India brings together leading researchers, security practitioners and industry decision makers for four days of cutting-edge research, technical exchange and strategic dialogue.

13 Trainings delivered by 19 trainers, 70+ Summit speakers, 200+ CXOs, CISOs and VIP buyers, and 2,000+ Business Hall delegates across four days.

Black Hat Arsenal featured 44 open-source security tool demonstrations across 32 workstations and four hands-on labs.

Keynotes by leading cybersecurity experts Dr. Sanjay Bahl, Director General, Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) and Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA), and Nathan Hamiel (Kudelski Security), alongside a special address by Shri Rajesh Kumar, IPS, Chief Executive Officer, Indian Cybercrime Co-ordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India.

Key themes included AI security, digital payment fraud, emerging cyber threats and post-quantum readiness.

Bengaluru, November 5, 2026 — Black Hat India 2026, organised by Informa Markets in India, concluded its inaugural edition at the Sheraton Grand, Brigade Gateway, Bengaluru, following four days of high-impact training, leadership discussions, original technical research and industry engagement from October 27 to 30, 2026.

Related:Japan Pushes Emergency Funding for Cybersecurity as AI-Assisted Breaches Rise

Founded in 1997, Black Hat is one of the world's most respected cybersecurity conference series, renowned for its independent, vendor-neutral research and technical depth. Its debut in India marks a significant milestone for the country's cybersecurity ecosystem, bringing a globally recognised platform and its international community of researchers and practitioners to one of the world's fastest-growing digital economies.

The inaugural edition brought together a diverse mix of technical training, strategic discussions, cutting-edge research and hands-on engagement, with each day offering a distinct experience for the cybersecurity community.

Day 1 opened with specialised Trainings, featuring 13 hands-on courses delivered by 19 trainers and covering subjects ranging from offensive security fundamentals to securing emerging AI systems.

Day 2 was dedicated to Summit Day, bringing together 70+ speakers and 200+ CXOs, CISOs and VIP buyers across two tracks, Frontier AI Security and CISO Strategy. Discussions examined the changing cybersecurity landscape, enterprise risk and the growing strategic responsibilities of security leaders.

Days 3 and 4 featured the Briefings and Business Hall, with 35 researchers and practitioners presenting original work on emerging threats, software and cloud security, AI and digital identity, while welcoming more than 2,000 Business Hall delegates. A major attraction was Black Hat Arsenal, where 44 presenters demonstrated open-source security tools across 32 workstations and four hands-on labs, enabling attendees to engage directly with developers and explore practical security applications.

Related:PwC's CISO on AI, Robots & What's Next for Security

The event brought together prominent government representatives, industry leaders and international cybersecurity experts. Summit Day was inaugurated in the presence of Lt. Gen. Rajesh Pant and Lt. Gen. M.U. Nair, both former National Cyber Security Coordinators of India; Dr. Sanjay Bahl, Director General, Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) and Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA); and Brijesh Singh, IPS, Principal Secretary, Government of Maharashtra.

Dr. Bahl's keynote examined the implications of emerging AI technologies for India's digital ecosystem and the importance of strengthening cyber resilience. Nathan Hamiel, Senior Director of Research at Kudelski Security, delivered the Briefings keynote, exploring how AI is transforming cybersecurity and why human expertise remains indispensable. Shri Rajesh Kumar, IPS, Chief Executive Officer, Indian Cybercrime Co-ordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India, delivered a special address on transnational cybercrime.

Related:NIST: Solo Shouldn't Mean Less Secure

Senior representatives from NPCI, the Reserve Bank of India, NCIIPC, PhonePe, CRED, Razorpay, Groww, Reliance, Adani Enterprises, HCLTech, EY, Deloitte, KPMG, Microsoft, Mandiant, Akamai, Zscaler and Zoho participated alongside independent and academic researchers.

Across the programme, discussions consistently highlighted the growing importance of securing and governing AI, the increasing sophistication of cyberattacks, software supply-chain vulnerabilities, digital payment fraud and deepfakes. Protecting India's Digital Public Infrastructure, preparing for post-quantum technologies and translating technical risks into business priorities also emerged as important themes.

India's rapid digital expansion is creating unprecedented opportunities, alongside an increasingly complex cybersecurity landscape. The average organisational cost of a data breach in India reached ₹25.5 crore in 2026, nearly 16% higher year on year, underlining the growing economic implications of cyber risk.

Commenting on the significance of Black Hat India's successful maiden edition, Mr. Yogesh Mudras, Managing Director, Informa Markets in India, said, "India’s rapid digital transformation has unlocked extraordinary opportunities, while also bringing the need to secure an increasingly connected economy into sharper focus. In the last financial year, UPI processed over 24,000 crore transactions worth more than ₹314 lakh crore, while CERT-In reported over 29.4 lakh cybersecurity incidents in 2025, an increase of approximately 44% over the previous year. The recent spate of global cyber incidents, including critical PHP vulnerabilities, being described as ‘Black October’, is a timely reminder that digital growth must be matched by stronger security and resilience.

The successful debut of Black Hat India is a significant achievement for us and an important addition to India’s cybersecurity ecosystem. The scale of participation and quality of discussions reflect the strong appetite for a platform of this calibre. As AI reshapes the threat landscape, staying ahead of emerging risks becomes even more critical. We are proud to have brought this globally recognised platform to India and look forward to building on this strong beginning,” he added.

The inaugural edition was supported by Diamond Partners TrendAI, Upwind and EY, alongside other sponsors and exhibitors, and shaped by the Black Hat India Review Board.

Black Hat India's debut comes in a milestone year for Informa Markets in India, marking 20 years of its presence in the country. The edition is also part of Festivity of Business, the company's annual campaign, now in its seventh year. Spanning 100 days, the campaign celebrates the optimism, energy and entrepreneurial spirit driving India's growth, bringing together the country's vibrant festive season and its high season of business events.

The successful inaugural edition establishes a significant new platform for India's cybersecurity community, bringing global expertise, original research and industry leadership together at a time when securing the digital future has never been more important.

For more information, visit www.blackhat-india.com.

Black Hat India extends the globally recognised Black Hat platform to India's rapidly evolving cybersecurity landscape in Bengaluru, connecting the country's growing community of information security professionals with global research, expertise and industry developments. The platform brings together cybersecurity practitioners, researchers, technology leaders and organisations to exchange knowledge, examine emerging security challenges and explore advancements in information security. Through its technical Briefings, specialised Trainings and industry engagement, Black Hat India provides opportunities for professional development, collaboration and knowledge sharing, while strengthening connections between India's cybersecurity ecosystem and the global security community.

Founded in 1997, Black Hat is an internationally recognized cybersecurity event series providing the most technical and relevant information security research. Black Hat inspires professionals at all career levels, encouraging growth and collaboration among academia, world-class researchers and leaders in the public and private sectors. Today, Black Hat Briefings and Trainings are held annually in the United States, Europe, and Asia, providing premier venues for elite security researchers and trainers to find their audience.

#9795. Jun Kim, oMLX creator and maintainer, joins Hugging Face to support the MLX community

We are super excited to welcome Jun as our newest team member 🔥. We are completely invested in local AI, and MLX is a central piece of the ecosystem. We are delighted that Jun chose us to set up home and continue contributing to MLX.

MLX is Apple's framework for local AI, especially optimized for Apple Silicon. We are big MLX supporters since it was the Christmas present from Awni and Angelos in 2023, and proud that Hugging Face is the Hub where people find MLX models and contribute their own. Usage of open, local AI is accelerating, and we believe in a healthy ecosystem where people can find the tools that work for them.

Stability, and hopefully faster development! Graduating from a side job to a fully maintained and funded project will allow Jun to better guide the contributors and build for the long-term. oMLX stays Apache 2.0, and Jun keeps leading it as before.

Our end goal is to unblock the community to run local AI in any shape or form, and provide the tools and building blocks to make that happen. We expect oMLX to serve as a testbed for new ideas, while leveraging the foundational work of the dependencies it already relies upon, such as mlx-lm or mlx-vlm. We believe that strong modeling and inference libraries help the community, so we'd love to upstream work to wherever it makes sense. We have been collaborating with many projects mlx-lm, mlx-vlm, LMStudio, and we hope we can strengthen the relationship with Cheng, Prince, Yagil, and their teams to better serve the community together.

Concretely, one focus area is the quick transition from a transformers model definition to a reference MLX implementation that can be consumed by different engines, so each one can focus on the unique features they provide. The transformers library has become the reference for ML model definitions, we want to streamline the process to make new transformers models run on MLX.

We are incredibly excited about the future.

#9794. Transformers now runs llama.cpp quants

We're adding support for running GGUF models efficiently in transformers, so you can use checkpoints sized for your laptop's memory through the familiar transformers APIs. Pick a GGUF from the Hub, load it with from_pretrained, and start generating on your own machine.

Running AI models on your laptop has become much easier, and llama.cpp has been a big part of that. Its inference engine powers local AI tools such as Ollama, LM Studio, and Jan. Alongside projects like MLX, it has helped make local inference a practical option for everyday use.

A recent example of what local AI can feel like:

This is where we are right now. And i’m not gonna lie it feels pretty magical 🧙‍♀️Qwen3.6 27B running inside of Pi coding agent via Llama.cpp on the MacBook ProFor non-trivial tasks on the @huggingface codebases, this feels very, very close to hitting the latest Opus in Claude… pic.twitter.com/lsIxLoUneU

GGUF, developed by the llama.cpp team, is a widely used format for local inference. The team also shares quantized checkpoints under ggml-org on the Hub. Publishers such as Unsloth, LM Studio Community, and bartowski also provide ready-to-use GGUF checkpoints in a range of quantizations, so users can pick the version that fits their machine. GGUF models have been downloaded millions of times.

We want to make it easier to run these models locally with transformers, too. Compatibility is only useful if the model is pleasant to run. To bring performance close to llama.cpp, we're reusing its underlying ggml kernels through the kernels library, and reducing overhead in generate. Our initial focus is local inference on Apple Silicon, starting with the Qwen3.5 architecture.

GGUF packages model weights and metadata, including tokenizer information and an optional chat template, in one file. It supports different quantization levels, letting you trade some precision for a smaller memory footprint. Variants such as Q4_K_M mix tensor precisions, using mostly 4-bit weights while keeping sensitive tensors at higher precision.

Here's how quantization changes the file size of Unsloth's Qwen3.5-4B:

We suggest starting with Q4_K_M, then trying Q5_K_M or Q6_K if you have more memory available. More aggressive quantization can help larger models fit, but the quality tradeoff depends on the model and the task. Evaluate it on the work you actually want the model to do. The Hub's GGUF documentation describes the available quantization types.

To load a GGUF model, pass its Hub model_id and filename as gguf_file to from_pretrained.

No extra configuration is needed: when the weights stay packed on Metal, transformers automatically loads the compatible ggml/Metal layer kernels and uses ggml-org/ggml-attn as the attention implementation. If that kernel cannot be fetched, the model falls back to "sdpa" with a warning, and you can always force "sdpa" by passing attn_implementation="sdpa" explicitly. See the GGUF documentation for more loading options.

That is the only GGUF-specific step. Everything after it is the standard transformers API:

Without a compatible quantization kernel, the loader falls back to dequantizing the model and uses more memory.

You can also use the same checkpoint with transformers serve, which exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:

The model argument uses :.gguf: before the colon is the Hub repository (unsloth/Qwen3.5-4B-GGUF), and after it is the file to load (Qwen3.5-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf). This selects a specific quantization from a repository that may contain several.

For models whose chat template supports thinking, add --reasoning off to skip it or --reasoning on to enable it. The default, --reasoning auto, follows the chat template’s default. See the reasoning options for details.

You can connect a client such as Jan or Pi by adding a custom OpenAI-compatible provider with these settings:

transformers runs the model on your Mac, while the client provides the conversation interface. The same endpoint can be used by other clients that support this API.

Our reference for local inference performance is llama.cpp. The comparison below focuses on three GGUF checkpoints: a small dense model, a larger dense model, and a mixture-of-experts model.

The llama.cpp column comes from the llama-bench tool (build 5f55650a7, release b10200, Metal backend from ggml 0.18.0), run as llama-bench -m -p 0 -n 128 -r 3, which reports tg128: the token-generation rate over 128 decoded tokens, averaged across three repetitions, with prompt processing excluded. The transformers column is generate producing the same 128 tokens from a 12-token prompt, best of three warmed runs, and it includes prefill.

Measured on a MacBook Pro M2 Max, 32 GB unified memory, macOS 26.6, PyTorch 2.12.1, kernels 0.17.0, plugged in.

Transformers is close to llama.cpp across all three checkpoints. The chart uses the same measurements described above; it does not imply identical benchmark conditions, since the Transformers measurement includes prefill while llama-bench reports decode-only throughput.

When GGML and llama.cpp joined Hugging Face, we described their complementary roles: llama.cpp provides a foundation for local inference, while transformers provides a foundation for model definition. GGUF support brings those two closer together.

llama.cpp remains our recommended engine when your priority is efficient local inference. Its dedicated runtime, memory management, and broad hardware support are built around that goal. This integration gives developers a convenient way to work with the same GGUF checkpoints inside transformers:

For that last case, use GgufConfig(dequantize=True):

The bigger opportunity is bringing ggml's performance to models that llama.cpp does not support.

transformers already provides the PyTorch implementations of these architectures. With ggml kernels and quantization schemes available in PyTorch, we can work toward accelerating their supported operations without first implementing the entire model in llama.cpp. This is especially useful for new architectures, research models, and custom variants that may never receive a dedicated llama.cpp implementation.

That opportunity extends beyond the GGUF format itself. A kernel operates on tensors; it does not require the whole model to come from a GGUF file. The same building blocks can be integrated into other transformers models and loading workflows. This also opens a path to other modalities: computer vision models, audio models, and multimodal models could reuse compatible attention, normalization, and matrix multiplication kernels without first having a full implementation in llama.cpp. Each architecture still needs integration and validation; the initial GGUF examples here cover text generation.

We also wanted to show how far we can get while keeping the model and generation loop in Python. With the right kernels and an efficient generation loop, Python and PyTorch can deliver strong local inference performance. The kernels handle the heavy computation, while the generation loop keeps the GPU busy by avoiding unnecessary synchronization.

Our focus was to make eager execution fast without requiring torch.compile. For interactive use, we wanted a quick start and a steady stream of tokens, without compilation pauses or recompilation when input shapes change. The two main pieces of that work are the kernels and generate itself.

A kernel is a small program that performs an operation on the GPU. PyTorch supplies general-purpose implementations; a specialized kernel can do less work, combine several operations, or read quantized weights directly in their stored format.

The kernels library lets us distribute compatible builds of ggml's Metal kernels on the Hub and call them from transformers. That brings ggml's work into the PyTorch model without replacing the model with a separate inference runtime.

The first four packages build on ggml's kernels; the top-k kernel addresses a separate bottleneck in MoE routing. Together they reduce the GPU work needed for each generated token.

To show the contribution of the layer kernels, we compare the same packed GGUF checkpoints with and without them. The quantization kernel stays enabled in both configurations: disabling it would also change how weights are represented and would measure a different tradeoff.

Faster kernels only help if the GPU has work to do. During generation, the CPU schedules GPU operations and controls the loop that produces the next token. Reading a result back from the GPU can force the CPU to wait until queued operations finish. Repeating even a small wait for every token can noticeably reduce throughput.

Two changes address this in generate, which results in improvements for all transformers models (not just when running GGUF files):

These changes improve the generation loop around the model, so their usefulness extends beyond GGUF. They complement the kernel work: kernels reduce the cost of an operation, while fewer synchronization points let CPU scheduling and GPU execution overlap.

These measurements keep all layer kernels enabled; the bars isolate the changes to the generation loop.

The initial target is a single interactive conversation on Apple Silicon. There are a few boundaries to keep in mind:

If you have a GGUF model you would like to use in transformers, open an issue with the checkpoint and your use case. That will help us prioritize support for the models people are running locally.

We would like to thank Arthur Zucker for initiating this work and reviewing all of my PRs, and Cyril Vallez for the generate PRs. We are grateful to Sayak Paul, the llama.cpp team, and Bertrand Chevalier for their help integrating the kernels. We also thank Aritra Roy Gosthipaty and Pedro Cuenca for reviewing this blog post, and Lysandre Debut for overseeing the project.

#9793. Microsoft Fixes RCE Bug in Windows Paint After Weeks of Confusion

Last month, Microsoft disclosed a vulnerability in Microsoft Paint, but messaging regarding a patch was unclear.

Microsoft recently patched a remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in Windows Paint, though details regarding how to fix the flaw seemingly remained unsettled for nearly a month.

According to an advisory, the flaw, CVE-2026-83844, is an "out-of-bounds read in Windows Paint [that] allows an unauthorized attacker to execute code locally." It carries a high severity CVSS 3.1 score of 7.0.

The advisory offers few technical details for defenders. Microsoft said acquiring RCE requires local access, meaning hands-on-keyboard or a direct remote connection to the attacker's machine. Some user interaction is also required; altogether, this may explain why the attack is "only" high severity rather than a 9 or 10 CVSS, as is so often associated with RCE flaws. Microsoft has observed no exploitation reports to date, further marking exploitation as "less likely."

A Windows Paint patch is available now. The fixed version is 11.2609.401.0, and customers can see it under Paint > Settings > About.

Related:F-Secure Identifies 26 Ways AI Can Harm Consumers, and Where to Stop Them

A Microsoft spokesperson tells Dark Reading, "A security update for Paint is available through the Microsoft Store, and customers with automatic Store updates enabled are already protected. We recommend customers check they are on the latest version and install the available updates to remain protected." Customers can also manually apply the update via Microsoft Store App > Downloads > Check for updates.

CVE-2026-83844 is an unusual vulnerability for multiple reasons, beyond it being a high-severity Paint vulnerability capable of RCE.

As Brian Vitko, founder of device management software provider RFF, wrote in a blog post, Microsoft first disclosed the bug on Oct. 13, but there seemed to be no indication the reported fix (11.2605.91.0) was live, even as of Oct. 30. By Nov. 4, Vitko, the correct fixed version was listed in the security advisory (11.2609.401.0) but 11.2605.81.0 was the latest update available in the store. The correct version was added to the store on Nov. 6.

The original version of the advisory FAQ, according to Vitko's post, said the attack could possibly be exploited, "by sending a specially crafted packet to an affected service over the network."

But the latest version of the FAQ reads, "For example, when the score indicates that the Attack Vector is Local and User Interaction is Required, this could describe an exploit in which an attacker, through social engineering, convinces a victim to download and open a specially crafted file from a website which leads to a local attack on their computer."

Related:AI Makes Reverse Engineering Mainstream Software & Malware Far Easier

Vitko tells Dark Reading that this latter explanation aligns more with his expectations for a vulnerability targeting Windows Paint, and that the wording may just be the result of standardized Microsoft FAQ language than speaking directly to the vulnerability.

"Paint isn't something that listens on the network. When it was published, it was CVSS 8.1 with a network attack vector, and the FAQ talked about 'a specially crafted packet to an affected service over the network.' Microsoft changed that on Nov. 7: it's now 7.0, local, user interaction required, and the FAQ says an attacker 'convinces a victim to download and open a specially crafted file from a website,'" he says. "That makes a lot more sense for an image editor. Microsoft hasn't said anything more about the actual trigger."

Dark Reading asked Microsoft for additional information regarding the update timeline.

#9791. For the first time, a C++ standard failed to pass the national bodies

Local 'minimal viable product that everyone agrees on' tanks the C++ standard.

It looks like it happened! A historic first, for better or worse.

This is a sign that C++ is (still) struggling with its governance (see a previous article on cultural issues within C++ here). This is a big deal even if you do not care about programming languages. C++ is arguably the most important programming language in existence.

Your computer runs on C or C++. The web browser you are using to read this is written in C++. ~All programming languages depend on C++ (often through LLVM). Likewise, ~all websites with performance requirements (e.g. YouTube) depend on C++, ~all data storage, game engines, finance, etc.

In a world that is drowning in exciting new vulnerabilities in ~all software, the ability of C++ to change and adjust to changing times affects you.

Let’s take a step back and get an overview. The initial source was a post by Robert Seacord on LinkedIn:

In a comment, J. Daniel GarcÃ­a adds: “There were 12 countries that abstained. In several cases because they could not reach to a common position. That is another signal of a contested draft.”

Now, before we get into the facts: This is not a good look for C++.

There have been multiple fights over the future direction of the C++ language, but no C++ standard ever failed to be signed off by the national bodies.

The national body vote is considered to be a formality. By the time the vote reaches the national bodies all disagreements should’ve been sorted out by WG21 (Working Group 21, i.e. the C++ Standards Committee).

Truly controversial features should never make it this far, since they should never be added to the C++26 working draft in the first place. This is a sign of division in the C++ community, in some form or another, and completely independently of whether you agree with this result or not.

Here, “Added to the C++26 working draft” is essentially accepting the pull request. Everyone is working towards the C++26 release, and people contribute to it with papers. Papers lead to votes, which then lead to amendments of the draft. Finally (this is where we are) wording passes happen, and it gets signed off, rubber-stamped and released. Phrased like this, the ISO process sounds sensible enough, but trust me, it’s actually kind of a nightmare.

Needless to say, the debates are raging, with comments on all sides: So many discussions.

Quick explanation: The national bodies execute a single vote. To pass the national bodies, the draft has to meet two bars:

If the above posts are correct, then the draft failed to meet both bars. Twelve isn’t two-thirds of twenty, and nine is more than a quarter. Visualization:

In total, there were 20 P-members, and 22 total members (ignoring abstaining). I heard that the US abstained, but take that with a grain of salt.

tl;dr: WG21 voted to include Contracts in C++26. Several high-ranking members of WG21 are strongly opposed to Contracts, and so are several national bodies. The national body vote was the ’last resort’ place to prevent Contracts from being canonicalized as part of the C++ standard.

New keywords that replace assert macros with a standardized way to enforce runtime checks. Most importantly, you can add pre and post checks to ensure that all arguments and return values fulfill certain conditions.

Looks simple, right? You’d think so, but no!

First, due to issues with virtual functions, Contracts for virtual functions were already cut from the proposal.

Second, it’s not entirely obvious how this will interact with constexpr or function inlining.

Third, there are compile flags to selectively enable or disable the enforcement. E.g. “If a contract is violated, do you want to 1) kill the program, 2) call a ‘contract-violation handler’ and then kill the program, 3) log an error, 4) ignore completely (and not even perform the check, for performance reasons)?”

Big question: You compile your code with enforce and are linking a prebuilt library that pulls in the same dependency as you, but with Contracts set to ignore. This is fine according to Contracts. The linker gets to keep one of the copies. What happens? Do Contracts run or not? What if a call is inlined across translation units?

Is there even a way for the user to guarantee that checks always run? (The answer is no. What? You were hoping that this feature could be used to ensure certain checks guarding against Undefined Behavior would always run, no matter what? Don’t be silly—this is C++.)

Oh, did I mention that code inside of predicates is just standard C++, so the compiler is allowed to elide checks due to Undefined Behavior?

But do feel free to take it from the source: The “Contracts paper” can be found here, and if you read closely, you’ll find some funny statements that really ruffled some feathers:

It is ill-formed, no diagnostic required (IFNDR) if multiple first declarations for the same function are in different translation units that do not have the same sequence of function contract specifiers.

All of this leads to so many funny issues, some of which can be poorly summarized as “Well, who even knows whether your Contracts are even going to be enforced, this is C++, the compiler can do whatever it wants lol”.

If you think “Gee, this proposal looks rather complex and messy”, keep in mind that the Contracts paper was explicitly designed to be a minimal viable product that everyone would be able to agree on.

If you only faintly paid attention to C++, you might be going into this assuming that Profiles (aka Bjarne Stroustrup’s initiative to make C++ safer via magical fairy dust, also controversial and considered to be ‘impossible to implement’ by some) are the sticking point, but no, Profiles did not make it into C++26.

Oh, y’know, it’s just because that’s all everyone has been talking about.

Most obviously, the pro-Contracts camp released “Do not remove Contracts from C++26” on Oct 23rd, i.e. around the time when the national body ballot closed. Vinnie Falco (the most outspoken voice against Contracts) countered with “Do Remove Contracts From C++26” on the very same day1.

If you’ve been paying attention, there’s a whole trail of papers and events here.

We’ve got talks, and Bjarne Stroustrup, the creator of C++ himself, saying “it’s claimed to be a minimum viable product. It is not minimal. I don’t think it’s viable”.

We’ve got multiple papers, say “Contract Concerns”, “Contracts make C++ less safe — full stop!”, or “Contracts’ fundamental flaws” (all reasonably short) opposing the behemoth that’s the Contracts paper and its rationale document (put together, almost 300 pages).

We’ve had multiple votes. Most importantly (Hagenberg, Feb 15th, 2025), the vote to formally add Contracts to the C++26 working draft, turned out 100 in favor, 14 opposed, 12 abstain. The multiple votes to remove Contracts from the draft all failed, most recently in Croydon, which is also when an amendment to support a mechanism to ensure mandatory contract enforcement failed.

If your eyes are glazing over at this point, I don’t blame you!

The whole situation is a mess, and trying to keep track of it from the outside is a fool’s errand: You’re basically forced to track dry meeting notes, and read between the lines looking at the various drafts people are publishing. Don’t do it.

This is not Contracts’ first rodeo: A different version of Contracts was up for debate around 2018, and was kicked out not too long after. At this point SG21 (‘Study Group 21’) was formed, dedicated to revamping the Contracts concept to get us the new “Minimum Viable Product” that’s currently part of the draft.

The whole situation went back and forth, resulted in fourteen revisions on the Contracts paper, many comments from the national bodies during the process, and finally in some people explicitly calling for the national bodies to veto C++26. (We call that ’the nuclear option’. FYI, some of the people signing this are themselves sitting on national bodies.)

What you need to understand is that the Hagenberg vote (on adding Contracts to the working draft) was strongly in favor of Contracts. 100 in favor vs. 14 against is not a weak result. This makes it incredibly puzzling that this final vote failed so badly (12 for, 8 against is bad).

One narrative on what happened is the following:

“There’s a loud minority strongly opposing Contracts in C++26. This group includes people with a lot of influence, e.g. Bjarne Stroustrup. Some members of this group actively lobbied the national bodies to vote against Contracts, even though WG21 achieved alignment, and agrees that Contracts should ship in their current form.”

This agrees with the evidence we’ve seen (votes in favor, some people strongly opposed). Herb Sutter is suggesting this in his latest paper, see here. (Herb Sutter, for the record, was the chair of the C++ Committee and is (next to Bjarne) perhaps the second-most-important person anyone in the C++ world listens to.)

This is plausible, but I don’t believe it. Not entirely, anyway. Yes, lobbying happened, and Bjarne’s opinion is something people listen to. It’s possible it was the deciding factor, but if it was the deciding factor, then this is a sign that the process itself is broken, and puts undue value onto status.

Even Herb Sutter acknowledges that Contracts were contentious. In footnote 4 on his paper, anyway.

Some of the NBs that voted Disapprove had participated and had expressed concerns about contracts without having to be lobbied (importantly, those were the first-ever Disapprove votes on any C++ DIS).

In other words, before any lobbying happened we already had a historical first, the strongest ever NB disagreement with a draft.

Importantly, it looks to me as though the committee just repeatedly ignored the comments/feedback of the national bodies throughout the process, and then ran face-first into a wall at the vote.

If you think “Oh, you are saying that the committee is just straight-up incompetent and/or evil, then?” No, not really. The committee process is just such a mess that it semi-naturally leads to situations like this. The people working within this system have become so used to the process that they’re barely capable of seeing it.

(Over the years many people who did not find this process workable just left entirely. There’s a huge selection bias effect.)

Part of what makes the process bad is that it’s very “all or nothing”, and the process is so slow that working on the standard is painful for everyone. More on that later.

Anyway. I don’t believe that it’s all just the lobbying. The discussions were already way underway. Evidence:

Taking a look at “Do not remove Contracts from C++26”, it refers to the “23 NB comments on contract assertions”.

Taking a closer look at N5028 and N5031, we see the committee rejected at least one strong anti-Contracts comment from each of the following countries: Sweden, Spain, the United States, France, Romania, the Czech Republic and Finland.

These comments included multiple asks to not ship Contracts in their current form at all, resolve safety issues, make Contracts reliably non-ignorable, fix the const issues, and change it such that standard library hardening phrasing does not depend on Contracts.

What did the committee think? That all of these asks were completely irrelevant? Yeah, no shit people are going to vote against something or abstain if you ignore their concerns.

This was preventable! People told you ahead of time that they were strongly opposed! The national bodies played their part correctly here. They gave you feedback ahead of time, and then voted accordingly.

There were at least four comments asking specifically “Please do not make the work on ‘standard library hardening’ depend on the inclusion of Contracts into C++26.” As it stands, this coupling is still there, i.e. the comments were ignored.

In fact, now that the future of Contracts is shaky, the “Do not remove Contracts” paper includes the following line:

At the time of writing, there is no wording for removing contract assertions from C++26, and producing it is not a purely mechanical exercise. It would require:

removing or respecifying C++26 standard-library hardening [P3471R4], which is written in terms of contract assertions and has never had complete, reviewed wording that is independent of contract assertions.

The audacity. The national bodies were very explicit in saying that they do not want standard library hardening to depend on Contracts.

You went and ignored those comments, and are now complaining about the effort that would be necessary to walk things back? You were given all the heads-up you needed, you just ignored it!

I quote Footnote 6 from Herb Sutter’s paper on the situation we are in. If there is an expert, it is him:

P3911 is the only technical proposal that NBs told us during CD comment processing would likely prevent multiple potential NB negative votes. Itâs also a pure extension that doesnât disturb the rest of the contracts design or interfere with future extensions, which makes it low-cost and low-risk to adopt. This is why in Kona I repeatedly encouraged EWG to pursue it. It addresses what several experts said was their principal concern motivated by safety issues: to provide a way to write a contract in source code that would be guaranteed to be enforced at execution time regardless of build mode or linking. However, it failed to be approved in the EWG 2026-01 telecon (âencourage more work in this directionâ failed by 8-25 for-against, with 9 neutral). Now we have the new information that NBs have rejected the DIS, and several have again cited safety as a critical issue, so this change is likely to increase NB consensus.

P3911 is the paper that proposes adding a way to ensure Contracts will always run, and can be enforced.

(Which, yes, a lot of people believe is necessary for a safety feature. If you can’t guarantee the safety is even enforced, what’s the point?)

Honestly, probably not. Herb Sutter is looking at the situaation from the political angle, and analyzing whose beliefs have more weight based on their status.

Bjarne Stroustrup’s beliefs (as the creator of C++) hold a lot of weight. This is correct.

Quoting Herb Sutter’s discussion on the matter:

Over half of the NBs that voted Disapprove on the C++26 DIS had never participated in WG21 at all and/or never before expressed any concern about contracts in C++26 (most sent no comments on the C++26 CD comment ballot; one sent contracts-unrelated CD comments), yet voted against the DIS after being lobbied with messages citing Bjarneâs opposition.

“Look! It’s just Bjarne having a lot of status!” he says, and he is completely right in saying so, but he is also acting as though putting huge pressure on members to “disagree and commit :-)” hadn’t always been part of it. The C++ Standards Committee always voted in terms of factions.

It was always a political mess where Bjarne’s explicit support was absolutely critical, and where “I know you may disagree with this, but you should vote in favor to get it in” was a part of the process.

Quoting Herb Sutter and Bjarne, yet again from Herb Sutter’s paper:

(Ed.: Bjarne added, when reviewing this paper, that one reason previous DIS ballots were unanimous was his private and public encouragement.)

Why are Contracts authors so obsessed with getting Contracts into C++26? Why not wait for the next release?

Well, C++ has this funny “release train model” (also known as “the frame rule bus stop analogy” in Super Mario Bros. speedrunning). A new version of the C++ standard releases every three years. If your work gets voted into the standard in time, it becomes part of it. If it doesn’t, you have to wait another three years for the next release.

Three years is a long time, and it’s an especially long time to work on a single C++ feature. Getting a C++ paper accepted into the standard is a process so notoriously draining that ~all of the “C++ people” I know just stopped bothering, and stopped working with WG21. It’s bad.

If Contracts don’t get in this cycle, there’s a good chance they never will. They will be nitpicked over the next three years, endlessly litigated, and frankly, I think there’s a good chance several of the people working on Contracts just won’t want to deal with that, and might instead drop out of the process entirely, leaving Contracts dead and buried.

Until the process itself changes, which, god knows how that could happen considering the requirements presumably imposed by ISO, it’s hard to imagine this changing.

This is why the pro-Contracts side released the following statement in their paper:

If the DIS ballot has failed, we should seek another ballot without altering contract assertions or removing them from C++26;

In other words, they are playing a game of Chicken: “We believe you are going to give up first.”

They know full well that a failed C++26 will hurt everyone. But, because the WG21 process is so insane that a loss here risks killing Contracts entirely, and would require another three years of endless litigation and fights, the stakes are high.

As far as I know, the next scheduled WG21 meeting runs Nov 16â21, 2026 in BÃºzios. So, you might think “Ah, then it’s just a few days and they’ll sit down and sort things out, right?”

Well, probably not. The WG21 + ISO process is slow and messy. Even if everyone agrees on whether Contracts should/should not go in, each ballot is open for multiple weeks. So yeah, this may take another year or so.

If C++26 fails, I’ll pour one out. Not for you, but for the many, many people who tried to make you better, and failed3.

If you've made it this far, consider signing up for e-mail notifications, following along on Substack, or adding this blog to your RSS reader.

It’d be slightly easier to take Vinnie’s paper seriously if it didn’t contain Claude-isms like “The ‘purely additive’ claim turns the deferral into a dismissal” that make my eyes glaze over. There has been an uptick in AI usage within WG21, and not all of it has been responsible. ↩︎

Okay fine, there were some tiny concessions, P3878R1 decoupled parts of standard-library hardening from Contract observe mechanics. Still coupled to Contracts though, making it impossible to allow standard-library hardening to enter without Contracts getting in. In other words, the ‘standard-library hardening’ draft was written with the assumption that Contracts would definitely go in. ↩︎

This, for the record, will include the Contracts people (assuming Contracts fail). I am not a big fan of Contracts (for reasons unrelated to any of the discussion here), but I understand the case for them, and the people working on them are (like everyone else) victims of the process. ↩︎

InfoQ Homepage News Author Q+A: finprim is a Case for One Financial Validation Library in TypeScript

Nov 12, 2026 6 min read

finprim, which is an MIT-licensed TypeScript library that puts IBAN, BIC, card, sort code, VAT, routing number and loan calculations behind one API, has published its fifth release, 0.1.4. The repository has 81 stars.

InfoQ asked author Oluwatosin Adelaja what pushed him to build it, and where he wants it to stop.

Adelaja: Honestly, it came from doing the same work too many times. At Sprint Technology Solutions we had several products, and each one ended up with its own copy of the same financial validation, sort code checks in one place, IBAN formatting in another, card validation somewhere else, all written slightly differently by whoever got there first.

The moment it really landed for me was on a payout flow. We had account and sort code validation on the web side, and then the mobile app needed the same thing. Rather than share it, the validation got rewritten for mobile, and the two copies drifted. One of them was a little stricter than the other, so a bank detail that the web form accepted would get rejected on mobile, and we had people re-entering details that were actually fine. It took longer than it should have to track down, because nobody thinks to check whether two "identical" validators are actually identical. The fix was easy once we found it, but the real problem was that there were two of them at all.

I hit the same shape of thing again later building a daily pay feature for NHS workers, where the same rules needed to hold on web and on mobile. That is when I stopped treating it as a one-off chore and started thinking it should just be one library, written once and tested once, that any product could pull in and trust.

InfoQ: What was missing that justified a unified library rather than assembling existing single-purpose packages?

Adelaja: You can absolutely wire together a pile of single-purpose packages, and plenty of teams do. The problem is what you are left maintaining. Each package has its own API shape, its own types, its own idea of what a valid result looks like, and often its own dependencies. So you end up writing a layer of glue code just to make them agree with each other, and that glue becomes its own thing to test and keep working.

finprim's bet is that financial validation is coherent enough to live behind one consistent API. The same shape of input, the same shape of result, and the same typing approach across IBAN, sort code, card, VAT, all of it. And zero runtime dependencies, so there is no tree of other people's packages to audit or keep patched. For something sitting in the path of a payment, I wanted fewer moving parts, not more.

InfoQ: What concrete class of bugs do branded types prevent, and why not rely on plain runtime validation?

Adelaja: The bug class is the one where a string that was never validated gets used as if it had been. To the compiler, a validated IBAN and a random string are both just a string, so nothing stops you passing the wrong one into a function that assumes the value is good. It compiles fine, and then it fails at runtime, which in this domain means it fails in the middle of a live transaction.

Branded types close that gap. A validated IBAN comes back as its own distinct type, not a plain string, so if you try to use an unchecked value where a validated one is required, the compiler rejects it before the code ever runs. The runtime validation still happens, that does not go away. The branding just guarantees it actually happened and that nobody quietly skipped it on some code path. It moves a whole class of "we forgot to validate this one route" mistakes from production back to compile time.

InfoQ: For something handling payment data, how do you think about trust, what can you guarantee, and where do you draw the line?

Adelaja: The honest answer starts with being clear about what finprim is and is not. It validates and formats financial data. It does not store anything, it does not send anything over the network, and it does not process payments. No database, no telemetry, no outbound calls.

So the guarantees I can actually make are narrow and specific. It checks values against published standards, IBAN structure, checksum rules, card network ranges, and tells you whether they are well formed, deterministically, without logging the sensitive values it is handling. That last part is deliberate. You do not want account numbers or card numbers turning up in logs, so the library does not put them there.

Where I draw the line matters just as much. finprim does not tell you a payment is safe to make, it is not a compliance tool, and it is not a replacement for the checks your payment provider runs. It confirms the data is shaped correctly before it goes anywhere. Treating a validation library as more than that would be the real mistake.

InfoQ: How do you source and maintain the correctness of 80+ IBAN formats, VAT quirks and card ranges, and how is it tested?

Adelaja: The rules come from the published standards rather than from me guessing. IBAN is checked against the ISO 13616 country formats, card numbers use Luhn plus the published network ranges, VAT uses the documented per-country formats, and so on. Where there is an authoritative spec, that is the source of truth.

On testing, each validator runs against known-good and known-bad values taken from those reference sources, so the tests check behaviour against the standard, not just against themselves. Overall coverage is around 91% of lines and 88% of statements. The core validation modules are the most heavily covered, the IBAN, card, VAT, routing, BIC and sort code logic sits around 94% of lines with full function coverage, and the thinner coverage is in the optional React bindings rather than the validation itself. I would rather be straight about that split than quote one headline number, because the part that actually handles financial data is the part that is tested hardest.

Keeping it correct over time is mostly manual, I update the formats as the standards change, and this is one place the outside contributors have genuinely helped, because people using it in different countries spot edge cases I would never hit on my own.

InfoQ: SEPA and ACH generation is a big jump from validation into transaction generation. Where do you want finprim to end up?

Adelaja: That is a fair thing to push on, because generation is a genuinely different job from validation, and I do not want to pretend otherwise. Validating an IBAN is self-contained. Producing a SEPA credit transfer file or an ACH batch means taking on formatting rules, sequencing and a lot more responsibility for getting something exactly right that is going to be submitted to a bank.

Where I want finprim to sit is as a validation and formatting toolkit first. I am deliberately cautious about the generation side. If it does move into producing standard file formats, I would want that to be safe, well-tested generation of documented formats, not finprim turning into a transaction engine or a payments platform. I would rather it did one layer really well than spread itself thin doing a half version of what a payment provider already gives you.

Narrower tools exist, such as ibankit for IBAN and BIC alone, and on DEV a commenter called the Dinero.js approach solid while warning that teams get burned when a library's precision assumptions diverge from the processor's.

Adelaja is a senior full stack engineer. All five releases have stayed within 0.1.x, so upgrading has meant patch releases rather than code changes, and there is no dedicated migration guide, so the README and release notes are the reference.

#9788. How UK AISI and EvalEval Are Making Benchmark Results Reproducible

The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.

AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema. This next phase of the collaboration puts that shared infrastructure into practice.

As AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly important sources of evidence about model and system performance. Yet results are reported across many formats, platforms, and outlets, often without enough information to reproduce them. Running the evaluations again may itself be prohibitively expensive.

EvalEval's mission is to improve this ecosystem through a shared reporting schema, Every Eval Ever, and an open platform, Evaluation Cards, that brings evaluation results and the information needed to interpret them into a common structure.

This builds naturally on AISI's work to make evaluation more efficient through OptStop, more statistically rigorous through HiBayES, and more standardised in areas including transcript analysis and capability elicitation. Together, AISI and EvalEval are working to diagnose gaps in evaluation reporting and build shared infrastructure to close them.

Transcript-level transparency matters not only for reproducibility, but also for analysis and diagnosis. In this new phase of the collaboration, AISI is making publicly reported evaluation methods and findings available through Evaluation Cards where appropriate. The release includes verified results, context, and configuration information for the five benchmarks in the paper's main experiment:

These results cover six frontier models: Claude Opus 4, Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5, GPT-5.2, and GPT-5.4. The release also includes results from two related cyber evaluations—Cyber CTFs and The Last Ones—which use a different, partially overlapping set of models. The data accompany AISI's paper, How Inference Compute Shapes Frontier LLM Evaluation, which studies how benchmark performance depends on inference-time compute and evaluation protocol.

Performance on Humanity's Last Exam changes with evaluation protocol and inference compute. Each curve shows the cumulative share of attempted tasks solved within a given token count, using the earliest observed success per task. When models received correctness feedback from an oracle after each attempt, they continued to solve additional tasks as token use increased.

When results are openly released with setup information, researchers and practitioners can examine individual studies more closely and compare findings across the wider ecosystem. Where other reports lack these details, releases like AISI's provide verified reference points for interpreting evaluations in context—for example, by helping researchers understand how setup choices may influence reported performance. As more evaluators adopt EEE, open comparisons like these can support broader and more reliable meta-research.

AISI's Terminal-Bench 2.0 results alongside other reported evaluations for the same models, under different evaluation setups.

We are excited about this adoption and look forward to further standardising and sharing evaluations with AISI and other AI evaluation organisations.

The EvalEval Coalition is a research community developing scientifically grounded research and robust deployment infrastructure for the evaluation ecosystem. Its goal is to improve evaluation science, address the lack of consensus around documenting evaluation applicability and utility, and broaden coverage of the impacts that matter for scientific research and policy analysis.

The coalition's flagship projects include Every Eval Ever, a shared schema and repository for evaluation results, and Evaluation Cards, which combines benchmark metadata, evaluation-run data, and model metadata into interpretable records. Together, they make it easier to understand when apparently similar scores were produced under meaningfully different conditions.

The UK AI Security Institute is a research organisation within the UK government's Department for Science, Innovation and Technology. Its mission is to equip governments with a scientific understanding of the risks posed by advanced AI. AISI conducts research and builds infrastructure to understand advanced AI capabilities and impacts, develop and test mitigations, and inform policy.

The line that matters for practitioners is quiet: apparently similar scores can be produced under meaningfully different conditions.

Once you've watched a benchmark move just by changing inference-time compute or the elicitation protocol, "Model A beat Model B on X" without a card is marketing, not comparison. Evaluation Cards that ship verified results with configuration — especially transcript-level context where it's appropriate — are how eval becomes a contract instead of a leaderboard screenshot.

One ask I'd put to teams adopting EEE: which fields get skipped first under deadline pressure (seed, tool access, attempt budget, oracle feedback), and do you treat a missing field as "do not cite the delta" rather than "assume defaults"?

Reproducible reporting won't remove disagreement. It will make the disagreement about the right variables.
